title: Tummy time on your chest
summary: Short tummy time sessions on your chest help a newborn get comfortable on their belly and start lifting their head.
how_to: Recline and lay your baby belly-down on your chest, facing you. Pat or stroke their back while you talk or sing. Gently turn their head now and then so they rest on each cheek equally. One or two minutes, several times a day, is enough at this age.
safety_notes: Awake and supervised only; stop for a break if your baby cries or tires. Always put your baby to sleep on their back. Keep your baby's nose and mouth clear; don't do this if you are drowsy.

title: Side-lying neck stretch under a mobile
summary: Lying on their side under a slow-moving mobile helps your baby stretch out of the curled womb position and turn their head.
how_to: Hang a mobile about 8 to 12 inches from your baby. Lay them on their side with their head beneath it, one hand on their hip or a rolled blanket at their back. Spin the mobile gently to catch their attention. Switch sides so both sides of the neck get stretched.
safety_notes: Stay with your baby the whole time; remove the rolled blanket afterwards. Hang securely and out of reach, never over the crib or sleep space; use only during supervised awake time and remove once your baby can grab it.

title: Floor time on a movement mat
summary: A few minutes of free movement on a firm mat when your baby is fed, changed and calm.
how_to: When your baby needs nothing (fresh diaper, fed, calm), lay them on their back on a firm mat or quilt on the floor. Let them stretch and wiggle freely, with a low mirror or a high-contrast image nearby. End when they need you; 5 to 10 minutes is typical for a newborn.
safety_notes: Use a firm, flat surface; keep pets and siblings at a distance. Floor time is for awake periods only.

title: Palm stroke for the grasp reflex
summary: Brushing your finger across your baby's palm triggers their grasp reflex, an early step toward hand control.
how_to: Hold your baby or lay them on their back. Gently brush a finger across their palm and let them close their hand around it. Try both hands. Repeat a few times while you talk to them.
safety_notes: Keep your nails short and smooth.

title: Keep hands uncovered
summary: Leaving your newborn's hands free lets them feel their own face and body, which leads to later hand discovery.
how_to: Skip scratch mittens and long sleeves that cover the hands when you can. During awake time, let your baby bring their hands to their face and mouth. Watch for small hand movements and let them happen.
safety_notes: Trim your baby's nails regularly to prevent scratches.

title: Face-to-face conversation
summary: Talking to your newborn face-to-face builds the foundation for language even before they understand.
how_to: Hold your baby 8 to 12 inches from your face and make eye contact. Speak in a high, expressive voice about anything: your day, what you see. Pause as if waiting for a reply.
safety_notes: Follow your baby's cues; if they look away or fuss, give them a break.

title: Real words during care
summary: Use clear, real language and describe what you are doing, so your baby hears rich speech from day one.
how_to: During diapering, dressing or feeding, tell your baby what is happening in plain words: "I'm going to pick you up now. Are you ready?" Pause after questions before acting. Avoid nonsense words; full, natural sentences are best.

title: Paper ripping sounds
summary: Slowly ripping or crumpling paper gives your newborn a new, interesting sound to notice.
how_to: With your baby in a quiet, alert state, hold a piece of scrap paper in their view. Rip or crumple it slowly. Watch for a startle, stillness or a change in their face. Keep it to one sound at a time.
safety_notes: Keep paper scraps out of your baby's reach afterwards; avoid sudden loud noises close to their ears.

title: Skin-to-skin time
summary: Holding your baby skin-to-skin calms them, helps regulate temperature and builds your bond.
how_to: Undress your baby down to the diaper and hold them against your bare chest, with a blanket over you both. Feeding time works well. Have water and your phone handy in case they fall asleep. Any caregiver or a supervised sibling can do this.
safety_notes: If you might fall asleep, move your baby to their own firm, flat sleep space first.

title: Holding on a topponcino
summary: A topponcino is a thin, firm pad that keeps your newborn's surface and smell consistent as they are held and passed between people.
how_to: Sleep with the topponcino for a few nights before birth so it smells like you. Hold your baby on it, or let relatives and siblings hold the baby on it. The surface stays the same when you set your baby down or pick them up, which helps them stay calm.
materials: topponcino (or a small, firm quilted pad)
safety_notes: Not a sleep surface: move a sleeping baby to a firm, flat crib or bassinet. Sit siblings down and supervise when they hold the baby.

title: Gaze into each other's eyes
summary: Short bouts of eye contact help your baby learn to tolerate faces and pick up social cues.
how_to: Hold your baby within 8 to 12 inches of your face. Look into their eyes for a few seconds and smile. Watch their face; when they look away, let them rest before trying again.
safety_notes: Eye contact is intense for newborns; look-aways are normal breaks.

title: Munari mobile
summary: The first Montessori visual mobile: slow-moving black-and-white shapes your newborn can study.
how_to: Hang a Munari or Munari-style black-and-white mobile about 12 inches above your baby in their movement area. Lay them under it during calm awake time and let them watch. Move on to the Octahedron mobile when their interest fades, often around 7 weeks.
materials: Munari mobile (bought or DIY black-and-white paper shapes)
safety_notes: Hang securely and out of reach, never over the crib or sleep space; use only during supervised awake time and remove once your baby can grab it.

title: Simple black-and-white images
summary: High-contrast images help your newborn practise focusing and coordinating both eyes.
how_to: Hold a simple black-and-white card about 12 inches from your baby's face. Keep it still until they look away, then swap to a new one. Use them during tummy time, in the car and during alert periods.

title: Focus play with a rattle
summary: Holding and slowly turning a high-contrast rattle gives your newborn practice focusing on a 3D object.
how_to: Hold a black-and-white rattle or small toy 8 to 12 inches from your baby's face. Wait until their eyes settle on it. Turn it slowly so they see it from different angles.
safety_notes: Use a rattle sized for infants with no small or detachable parts.

title: Calming baby massage
summary: Gentle smoothing strokes relax your baby, can improve sleep and give you a calm way to connect.
how_to: Lay your baby on their back on a blanket in a warm room. Use slow smoothing strokes, not rubbing, from the chest out to shoulders, arms, hands, legs and feet. Use baby-safe oil if you like. Stop when your baby shows they have had enough.
safety_notes: Patch-test any oil on a small area of skin first. Keep the room warm. Skip it if your baby is very hungry, full or tired.

title: Light and dark play
summary: Opening and closing a curtain slowly lets your newborn's eyes practise adjusting to light.
how_to: Hold your baby near a window. Pull the curtain open slowly, pause, then close it. Watch their eyes respond. At other times keep lights low and raise them gradually.
safety_notes: Avoid direct sunlight or bright lights in your baby's eyes.

title: Read a high-contrast book
summary: Reading together from the first weeks makes books a warm, familiar experience.
how_to: Hold your baby close and open a book with bold black-and-white pictures. Read it, or just talk about the pages. Slowly turn the book or stand it up like a tent for them to look at. Stop whenever they lose interest.

title: Tummy time across your thighs
summary: Lap tummy time with a high-contrast card gives your baby a reason to lift their head.
how_to: Sit and lay your baby belly-down across your thighs, head supported, and rub their back. Raise one leg slightly so they can see a bit more. Hold a high-contrast card in their line of sight and slowly move it upward to invite a head lift. This builds on chest tummy time from the newborn weeks.
safety_notes: Awake and supervised only; stop for a break if your baby cries or tires. Always put your baby to sleep on their back.

title: Leg push and gentle bicycling
summary: Pressing against your hand and slow leg bends help your baby build leg strength and get used to kicking.
how_to: With your baby on their back, place your hand and forearm against the soles of their feet and let them push. Then slowly bend and straighten their legs one at a time at the hip and knee. Keep movements gentle and follow their lead.
safety_notes: Never force a stretch; stop if your baby resists or fusses.

title: Tummy time with the Look at Me Ladybug
summary: A toy ladybug that click-clacks down a ramp gives your baby sound and motion to lift their head toward.
how_to: From about 4 to 6 weeks, set the ramp on a firm surface 8 to 12 inches in front of your baby during tummy time. Let the ladybug roll down and watch for a brief head lift. Two to five trips is plenty before a break. You can also show it while your baby is on their side or on your lap.
materials: Look at Me Ladybug (Lovevery Looker Play Kit)
safety_notes: Awake and supervised only; stop for a break if your baby cries or tires. Always put your baby to sleep on their back.

title: Black-and-white mittens for hand discovery
summary: Patterned mittens make your baby's hands easier to see, which can help them notice their hands sooner.
how_to: Lay your baby on a plain blanket with nothing else high-contrast nearby. Put black-and-white mittens on their hands, or loosely tie a patterned cloth around each palm. Watch whether they notice their hands; if not, gently move a hand into view.
safety_notes: Tie cloth loosely, never around wrists or fingers tightly; remove after play and supervise throughout.

title: Ring in the hand
summary: Placing a light ring in your baby's palm engages the grasp reflex with an object instead of your finger.
how_to: Stroke the back of your baby's hand to help it open. Place a lightweight ring in their palm and let their fingers wrap around it. Cup your hand gently over their fist to help them hold on for a few seconds. This is the next step after the newborn palm-stroke game.
safety_notes: Use a ring made for infants, too large to fit in the mouth whole; supervise.

title: House tour
summary: Carrying your baby room to room while you describe what you see gives them lots of words and new sights.
how_to: When your baby is awake, carry them in your arms or a carrier and walk slowly through your home. Stop at windows, plants and pictures and name what you see. Keep your voice warm and unhurried.
safety_notes: Support your baby's head and neck; check carrier fit and that their airway is clear.

title: Everyday sound tour
summary: Introducing household sounds one at a time teaches your baby that objects and people make sounds.
how_to: With your baby alert and the room quiet, make one sound at a time: tap a window, ring the doorbell, press microwave buttons, run a hairdryer briefly. Name each sound. This extends the single paper-ripping sound from the newborn weeks to a range of real-life sounds.
safety_notes: Keep loud appliances at a distance from your baby's ears; stop if they startle and cry.

title: Make-up songs for care routines
summary: Singing the same simple songs during care helps your baby calm down and hear the rhythm of language.
how_to: Pick a familiar tune and make up words about what you are doing: "Diaper changing, diaper changing, nice and clean" to "Are You Sleeping?" Hold your baby against your chest when you can so they feel the vibration. Repeat the same few songs daily, especially at wind-down time.

title: Encourage social smiles
summary: Smiling, eye contact and repeating what made your baby smile help those first social smiles grow.
how_to: Make frequent eye contact and smile at your baby. If a funny sound gets a smile, say "That silly sound made you smile! Should I do it again?" and repeat until they lose interest. Don't try to coax smiles when your baby is upset; comfort them instead.
safety_notes: Social play can overwhelm quickly; stop when your baby squirms or looks away.

title: Calm-down toolkit
summary: Rocking, shushing and gentle face strokes use your calm to help a fussy baby settle.
how_to: After checking for hunger, burps and diaper, try one technique at a time: rock with varied speed and direction, shush close to their ear matching then lowering their volume, take a walk with baby facing out, or stroke from forehead down the nose and over each eyebrow. Note what works; it can change day to day.
safety_notes: If you feel frustrated, put your baby down safely in the crib and take a short break. Never shake a baby.

title: Face tracking on your lap
summary: Your face is the most interesting thing to your baby; slowly leaning side to side invites them to follow it.
how_to: Sit with your knees up and lay your baby on your thighs, nestled where your legs meet, facing you. Keep your face within 12 inches. Slowly lean your head to one side, then the other, and watch whether their eyes follow.
safety_notes: Support your baby's head with your thighs or hands.

title: Octahedron mobile
summary: The second Montessori visual mobile: three shiny octahedrons in red, blue and gold as colour vision begins.
how_to: When your baby's interest in the Munari mobile fades (often around 7 to 8 weeks), swap in an Octahedron mobile in the same spot about 12 inches above them. Let them watch during calm awake time on their mat. Notice whether the change catches their attention.
materials: Octahedron mobile (bought or DIY metallic paper)
safety_notes: Hang securely and out of reach, never over the crib or sleep space; use only during supervised awake time and remove once your baby can grab it.

title: Side-to-side visual tracking
summary: Slowly moving a high-contrast object across your baby's view helps them practise following with their eyes.
how_to: Hold a black-and-white card or rattle 8 to 12 inches from your baby's face; jiggle it to get their attention. Once they focus, move it very slowly left to right, then back. If they lose it at the middle, stop and let them find it again. A few minutes is enough.
safety_notes: Watch for tiredness cues (yawning, looking away) and stop.

title: Low mirror by the movement mat
summary: A mirror placed low beside your baby's mat gives them a wider view of the room and of their own movements.
how_to: Lean or fix a shatter-resistant mirror horizontally along the wall next to the movement mat, at floor level. Lay your baby beside it during awake floor time and let them look. Some babies stare for long periods; others take weeks to get interested.
safety_notes: Use shatter-resistant glass or non-distorting acrylic and secure it so it can't tip. Don't place it beside a sleep space.

title: Daily outdoor walk
summary: A daily walk outside gives your baby fresh air, natural light and new sights, sounds and smells.
how_to: Take your baby out in a bassinet stroller or carrier once a day. Pause under trees so they can watch leaves move. Describe what you hear and see. Short walks count.
safety_notes: Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun (shade and a hat; no sunscreen). Dress for the weather and avoid long outings over 90F/32C.

title: Show the clothes before dressing
summary: Showing your baby each piece of clothing before you put it on is a first step in Montessori practical life.
how_to: Choose an outfit, then hold each item in front of your baby and name it: "Here is your blue shirt." Tell them what you are about to do, pause, then dress them slowly. A small set of easy front-opening clothes makes this simpler.
safety_notes: Choose clothes with front snaps and no drawstrings or loose decorations.

title: Temperature play with cotton balls
summary: Brushing on cool and warm damp cotton balls gives your baby an early sense of temperature differences.
how_to: Fill one bowl with cool water and one with warm. Dip a cotton ball in cool water and brush it gently over your baby's hand, then face and body, saying "Does this feel cool?" Test the warm water on your inner wrist, then repeat. Watch their expressions.
safety_notes: Test warm water on your wrist first. Never leave water within reach; put bowls and cotton balls away right after.

title: Side-to-back roll
summary: Following a toy up and behind them helps your baby practise rolling from their side to their back.
how_to: Lay your baby on their side on the floor. Hold a black-and-white object 8 to 12 inches from their face, then slowly move it up and behind them until they roll onto their back. Repeat a few times, then switch sides.
safety_notes: Use a firm, flat floor surface away from furniture edges.

title: Kicking play
summary: Giving your baby something to kick with their feet builds leg strength and an early sense of cause and effect.
how_to: With your baby on their back, tuck the edge of some tissue paper under a couch cushion near their feet so it crinkles when they kick. Or dangle a soft toy that rattles near their feet. Show them by gently touching their feet to it, then let them kick freely.
safety_notes: Stay with your baby; keep paper away from their face and remove it when play ends. Secure any hanging toy so it can't fall.

title: Upright holding for head control
summary: Holding your baby upright with only light head support lets them practise steadying their own head.
how_to: Hold your baby upright against your chest or facing you, with your hand ready behind their head. Give just enough support that they work a little to keep it steady. Expect some bobbing; it gets steadier with practice. Holding them upright over your shoulder works too.
safety_notes: Keep a hand close behind your baby's head at all times; their neck control is still developing.

title: Bell on a ribbon
summary: The first Montessori tactile mobile: a bell on a ribbon your baby can hit to make a sound.
how_to: When your baby starts reaching toward their visual mobile, hang a bell on a ribbon over the movement area within reach of their hands. Lay them under it and let them discover the sound when their arm hits it. Keep the visual mobiles for other times.
materials: bell on a ribbon (bought or DIY with elastic)
safety_notes: Strangulation risk: keep the ribbon short, attach with elastic so it gives when pulled, supervise every session and take it down after play. The bell must be too large to swallow and firmly attached.

title: Help the hands open
summary: Touch games help your baby's fists relax and open as they move from reflexes toward using their hands.
how_to: If your baby's hands are mostly fisted, stroke the back of each hand and watch for the fingers to open. Gently uncurl their fingers and thumb. Pat their hands together, or pat their hand on yours. Let them touch and pat your face.
safety_notes: Keep your touch light; never force fingers open.

title: Tissue paper batting
summary: A large sheet of tissue paper near your baby's arms and feet rewards their waving with a crinkly sound.
how_to: When your baby starts waving their arms (around 9 to 11 weeks), lay them on their back and position a large sheet of tissue paper where their hands or feet might hit it. Watch whether they notice the sound after an accidental hit and try again.
safety_notes: Stay right there; tissue paper is a suffocation and choking risk if it reaches the face or mouth. Put it away after play.

title: Copy your baby's coos
summary: Imitating your baby's first coos with eye contact and a smile encourages them to keep 'talking'.
how_to: When your baby makes an 'ahh' or 'ohh', look into their eyes, smile and repeat it back. Wait a few seconds for another sound. Diaper changes and bath time are good moments. Their attention may last only a minute or two.
safety_notes: Some babies find long eye contact overwhelming; follow their cues.

title: Pause and wait for a reply
summary: Leaving a pause after you speak gives your baby time to process and answer with a coo, smile or movement.
how_to: When you talk to your baby, stop after a sentence or question and wait several seconds longer than feels natural. Watch for any response: a sound, a smile, a kick. Respond to what they do, then pause again.

title: Find the sound
summary: Making a gentle sound out of view and slowly bringing it into sight helps your baby start to look for where sounds come from.
how_to: Clink two spoons, tear paper or shake a rattle to one side of your baby. See if they look around. If they don't, keep making the sound and slowly move it into their view. Try the other side.
safety_notes: Keep sounds gentle and away from your baby's ears.

title: Tell them what comes next
summary: Using the same words before routine actions helps your baby anticipate you and get excited when you approach.
how_to: Before picking up, feeding or changing your baby, say the same short phrase in the same tone each time, such as "Here I come to pick you up!" Pause, then do it. Over the coming weeks, watch for kicks, smiles or coos when they hear it.

title: Join them in tummy time
summary: Lying on your belly face-to-face with your baby turns tummy time into connection time.
how_to: Put your baby on a mat on their tummy, then lie on your belly facing them at eye level. Smile, talk and make eye contact. This moves tummy time from your chest to the floor, with your face as the reason to lift their head.
safety_notes: Awake and supervised only; stop for a break if your baby cries or tires. Always put your baby to sleep on their back.

title: Respectful care moments
summary: During diapering and bathing, look into your baby's eyes and talk them through each step instead of distracting them with toys.
how_to: Slow down during care. Look at your baby, tell them what you are doing ("Now I'm lifting your legs"), ask simple questions and wait. This builds on the plain-language narration from the newborn weeks by adding eye contact, pauses and small choices.
safety_notes: Keep one hand on your baby on any raised changing surface.

title: Gobbi mobile
summary: The third Montessori visual mobile: five spheres in graded shades of one colour that invite close looking.
how_to: When interest in the Octahedron mobile fades, hang a Gobbi mobile in the movement area, lightest sphere highest and darkest lowest. Let your baby watch during awake floor time. If they seem unsure, try again in a few days.
materials: Gobbi mobile (bought or DIY embroidery floss on balls)
safety_notes: Hang securely and out of reach, never over the crib or sleep space; use only during supervised awake time and remove once your baby can grab it.

title: Complex black-and-white cards
summary: Swapping in more complex patterns and new angles keeps your baby's eyes working as their vision improves.
how_to: Show a complex black-and-white card a few times in a row: wait until your baby looks away, then hold it up again when they look back. After a few repeats, rotate it or swap to a new card. This steps up from the simple cards used in the first weeks.

title: Tracking in new directions
summary: Once side-to-side tracking is smooth, move the object up, down and in circles.
how_to: Hold a high-contrast toy 8 to 12 inches away and move it slowly side to side to warm up. Then try up and down, or a slow circle. Try different positions: on their back, in tummy time, or held upright. Pause if they lose it.
safety_notes: Stop at yawns or look-aways; tracking is tiring.

title: Play silk to lie on
summary: Lying on a folded play silk gives your baby a new, moving texture to feel with their head, hands and feet.
how_to: Fold a play silk in half and lay it on the floor mat. Place your baby on top with head, hands and feet free. Keep everything else simple so they can focus on the feeling. Watch their face for calm interest.
safety_notes: Keep fabric flat and away from your baby's face; supervise and put it away after play.

title: Listen to a real instrument
summary: Hearing live music from real instruments exposes your baby to rhythm and a range of sounds.
how_to: Play a simple instrument such as a xylophone or drum near your baby, or let an older sibling play for them. Vary soft and lively, high and low. Play recorded music of different styles at other times, one sound source at a time.
materials: xylophone, drum or other simple instrument
safety_notes: Keep volume moderate and instruments away from your baby's face.

title: Pictures at the changing table
summary: High-contrast pictures beside the changing table give your baby something to look at and you something to talk about.
how_to: Put black-and-white pictures or decals next to the changing table at your baby's head level and slightly above. During changes, talk about what they are looking at: "You're looking at the tree." Swap pictures every week or two.
materials: black-and-white wall decals or printed pictures
safety_notes: Fix pictures firmly to the wall out of reach; keep one hand on your baby on the changing table.

title: Mirror tummy time
summary: A low mirror in front of your baby during tummy time gives them a face to lift up and look at.
how_to: Place a baby-safe mirror flat or propped low on the floor in front of your baby during tummy time, low enough that they have to lift their head to see it. Lie beside them so your face shows in the mirror too. As they get stronger, watch for them propping on their forearms.
safety_notes: Awake and supervised only; stop for a break if your baby cries or tires. Always put your baby to sleep on their back. Use an acrylic or shatter-resistant mirror and secure it so it can't tip.

title: Airplane game
summary: Lying on your shins while you rock your legs strengthens your baby's neck, back and core.
how_to: Lie on your back with knees bent to your chest. Place your baby face down along your shins and hold their hands or hold them around the waist. Sing, chat and make faces as you lift your legs and rock gently side to side.
safety_notes: Hold your baby securely around the trunk the whole time and move slowly. Skip it right after a feed.

title: Rolling bell in tummy time
summary: Rolling a bell toy across the floor in front of your baby makes them turn their head to follow the sound and movement.
how_to: During tummy time, slowly roll a rolling bell (or another chiming ball) across the floor in front of your baby, left to right and back. Let them turn their head to follow. Over the next months this head turning helps lead to rolling.
materials: rolling bell toy (Lovevery Charmer Play Kit or similar)
safety_notes: Awake and supervised only; stop for a break if your baby cries or tires. Always put your baby to sleep on their back. Check the toy has no small parts.

title: Basket of grasping rings
summary: Light rings in metal, wood and crochet are easy for a new grasper to hold and safe to mouth.
how_to: Keep two or three grasping rings in a small basket by the movement area. Place one in your baby's hand or on the mat within reach and let them explore it by hand and mouth. Rotate textures from day to day. This takes over from the single ring placed in their hand at one month.
safety_notes: Rings should be too large to fit fully in the mouth, with no loose parts. Wash regularly; supervise.

title: Batting at hanging toys
summary: When your baby starts swinging their arms at things, hang toys close enough for them to hit on purpose.
how_to: Move the bell on a ribbon lower so it is right at your baby's hands, or hang one simple toy from a play-gym bar. Lay your baby underneath and let them bat at it. This steps up from the accidental hits of the bell ribbon at two months to aimed swings.
materials: bell on a ribbon or simple hanging toy
safety_notes: Hang within easy reach but use elastic so it gives when pulled; check nothing can wrap around your baby. Supervise and take down after play.

title: Bell rattle
summary: A small wooden rattle with bells rewards your baby's grasp and hand movements with a soft jingle.
how_to: When your baby can bring their hands to their mouth, place a bell rattle in their palm. Let them hold, shake and mouth it. Watch for early attempts to move it from hand to hand.
safety_notes: Check that bells are enclosed or firmly fixed and can't come loose; don't use worn DIY rattles.

title: Lead a coo conversation
summary: Start the 'conversation' with a vowel sound, then copy and add to whatever your baby says back.
how_to: Sit face to face and say 'ahh' or 'ohh' with big, exaggerated lip movements in a high voice. If your baby answers, repeat their sound and add a new one. Pause a few seconds each time. This moves on from simply copying their coos to taking turns and adding sounds.
safety_notes: Follow your baby's cues; take a break if they turn away.

title: Copy-me faces
summary: Babies this age watch mouths closely; poking out your tongue or repeating their sounds invites them to copy you.
how_to: Hold your baby facing you, close enough to see your mouth. Slowly poke out your tongue, or repeat a sound they just made, then wait. Give them time to try it back. Tell them what you are doing as you go about the day, too.

title: Turn toward your voice
summary: Talking or singing from one side encourages your baby to turn their head toward your voice.
how_to: Lay your baby on their side with a rolled blanket behind their back, or on their back on the mat. Sit above or beside them and talk or sing so they turn toward you. Then move to the other side and repeat.
safety_notes: Supervise side-lying and remove the rolled blanket afterwards.

title: Gentle fun for first giggles
summary: Peekaboo, nose rubs and raspberries can bring out your baby's first laughs.
how_to: When your baby is rested and content, hide your face behind your hands and reveal it with a smile. Try rubbing noses, blowing raspberries on their tummy or making funny faces in a mirror. Notice what gets a smile or laugh and repeat it.
safety_notes: If your baby turns away or gets upset, switch to cuddling.

title: Reunion time
summary: Giving your baby a few minutes of full attention when you come home strengthens your connection.
how_to: When you return from work or time apart, spend 5 to 10 minutes with just your baby before starting chores. Read a book, go outside or sit together and tell them about your day. Put your phone away.

title: Faces in the mirror
summary: Making faces and naming face parts together in a mirror turns the mirror into a social game.
how_to: Sit with your baby in front of a mirror so both of your faces show. Make faces and have a 'conversation' with their reflection. Touch your nose, then theirs, naming each part.
safety_notes: Use a shatter-resistant mirror secured so it can't fall.

title: Wearable wrist rattles
summary: Soft rattles on your baby's wrists or ankles make a sound when they move, drawing their attention to their own hands and feet.
how_to: Fasten a soft wearable rattle loosely around one wrist or ankle while your baby lies on their back. Let them move and notice the sound. Watch whether they look at the hand or foot that jingles. Switch sides.
materials: wearable wrist/ankle rattles (Lovevery Charmer Play Kit or similar)
safety_notes: Fasten loosely enough to fit a finger underneath; check for loose parts and remove after play. Supervise.

title: Pause before the feed
summary: Showing the breast or bottle and naming it before feeding helps your baby anticipate food.
how_to: When your baby is hungry, hold them in the feeding position and show the breast or bottle. Say the same words each time, such as "Time for milk," and pause a moment before offering it. Watch for their mouth opening or excited movements.
safety_notes: Keep the pause short; don't delay a feed for a very hungry or upset baby.

title: Which picture do you like?
summary: Showing two pictures and following the one your baby looks at longer lets them show a preference.
how_to: Hold up two high-contrast or simple picture cards. Notice which one your baby keeps looking at and put the other away. Talk about the chosen card: describe it, ask a question and answer it yourself.

title: Herb tray
summary: A tray of fresh rosemary or other herbs gives your baby new smells and textures to reach for.
how_to: Put a few sprigs of rosemary on a tray on the floor. Lay your baby belly-down on a firm pillow or rolled blanket in front of it so their chest is lifted and arms are free to reach. Try mint, thyme or lavender another day.
safety_notes: Supervise closely: don't let your baby mouth the herbs or rest their face in the pillow. Put everything away after.

title: Splash tray for feet
summary: A shallow tray of warm water under your baby's bare feet encourages kicking and splashing.
how_to: Lay a towel on the floor or in a shady spot outside and put your baby on it, on their back. Place a shallow baking tray with a little warm water under their bare feet. Stir the water or drip it on their toes if they don't kick at first.
safety_notes: Use as little water as possible and stay within arm's reach; babies can drown in an inch of water. Test the temperature and empty the tray straight after.

title: Tree mobile
summary: Lying under a tree lets your baby watch leaves move, nature's version of a mobile.
how_to: Spread a blanket in the shade directly under a tree or bush and lay your baby on their back. Let them watch the leaves move and listen to the sounds. Bring a leaf close for them to feel and look at.
materials: a tree or bush in shade
safety_notes: Keep your baby in shade with a hat (no sunscreen under 6 months). Check for insects and falling debris; don't let them mouth leaves.

title: Airplane tummy time
summary: Progression from month 3's airplane game: your baby now holds the 'flying' pose longer, lifting head and chest while you rock.
how_to: Lie on your back with your knees bent toward your chest. Place your baby face down on your shins and hold their hands or support them around the waist. Sing, talk and make faces as you gently lift and rock your legs side to side. Compared with month 3, hold the position a little longer as head control improves.
safety_notes: Keep a firm hold around the trunk, move slowly, and do this on the floor so there is no fall height. Skip it right after a feed.

title: Crinkle paper kicking
summary: Tissue paper at your baby's feet rewards every kick with a crinkle, building the core strength used for rolling.
how_to: Lay your baby on their back near the couch. Wedge one edge of a sheet of tissue paper under a cushion so the paper hangs where their feet can reach it. Let them kick and discover the sound; reposition the paper if it slips.
safety_notes: Stay beside your baby and remove the paper afterwards; torn tissue paper is a choking risk if it reaches the mouth.

title: Bell on a ribbon
summary: Progression from the month-2 bell on a ribbon: hang it a little lower so your baby moves from batting it to grabbing and pulling it.
how_to: Hang a bell on a ribbon from a hook or play gym so it sits within arm's reach over your baby's chest. Lay your baby on their back below it and let them swing at it. Watch as accidental hits become deliberate swipes over the coming weeks.
safety_notes: Use a short ribbon with elastic, keep it out of reach of the neck, sew the bell on securely, and take it down when you are not right there.

title: Ring-in-hand grasping
summary: Help your baby move from a reflex grasp to holding a ring on purpose.
how_to: Stroke the back of your baby's hand to help it open. Place a small, light ring in their palm so their fingers wrap around it, and gently cup your hand over their fist to help them hold on. Let them bring it to their mouth.
materials: lightweight wooden or silicone grasping ring
safety_notes: Choose a ring too large to fit fully in the mouth with no small parts. Supervise mouthing.

title: Where's that voice?
summary: Talk to your baby from out of sight so they search for your voice.
how_to: While your baby is on their back or in a supported seat, walk toward them from where they can't see you and start talking. Keep talking as you come closer so they turn their eyes and head to find you. Greet them warmly when they spot you.

title: Pick a picture and talk about it
summary: Progression from month 3's picture preference: show two high-contrast cards, see which one your baby looks at longer, then talk about their choice.
how_to: Hold up two high-contrast or simple picture cards. Notice which one holds your baby's gaze and put the other away. Describe the picture they chose, ask a question and answer it yourself ('What does a dog say? Woof!').

title: Smile back and forth
summary: Respond to your baby's social smiles so they learn their smile gets a reaction.
how_to: When your baby is calm and alert, get face to face and smile. If a funny sound makes them smile, say so ('That silly sound made you smile! Again?') and repeat until they lose interest. If they are upset, comfort them instead of trying for a smile.
safety_notes: Take a break when your baby looks away or squirms; face-to-face play can overwhelm quickly.

title: Copy your baby
summary: Imitate your baby's faces, movements and sounds so they get more engaged with you.
how_to: Watch your baby closely. When they make a face, wave an arm or make a sound, copy it back playfully. Pause and see what they do next, then copy again.

title: Rattle socks for finding feet
summary: Bright socks or wrist rattles draw your baby's attention to their own hands and feet.
how_to: Put colourful socks or mittens with bells, or soft wrist rattles, on your baby. Lay them on their back so they can see and hear their limbs move. Let them grab, pull and suck on hands and feet.
materials: socks or mittens with bells, or soft wrist/ankle rattles
safety_notes: Check that bells are securely sewn on and remove the rattles for sleep.

title: Safe things to mouth
summary: Offer a few safe household objects so your baby can explore with their mouth, which also supports early speech.
how_to: Pick one or two items such as a silicone-tipped spatula, a metal or wooden spoon, a baby toothbrush or a partially frozen washcloth. Hand one to your baby while sitting with them and let them explore. Swap items to give new textures and temperatures.
safety_notes: Supervise closely: babies can gag on a handle pushed too far into the mouth. Do not offer keys, tissues or wipes.

title: No-mess paint bag
summary: Paint sealed inside a bag lets your baby squish colours around during tummy time.
how_to: Squirt four small blobs of non-toxic paint on white paper and slide it into a sturdy zip bag. Seal the bag with duct or painter's tape and tape all four sides to the floor. Lay your baby on their tummy with forearms on the bag and show them how to press and pat.
safety_notes: Supervise the whole time in case the bag splits, and put it away after play.

title: Talk-through diaper changes
summary: Use diaper and clothing changes to tell your baby what is happening and name body parts.
how_to: Set up the changing area so you stand at your baby's feet and they can see your face. Slow down and describe each step ('Now I'm lifting your legs') and name body parts as you touch them. Pause so your baby can respond with looks or sounds.
safety_notes: Keep one hand on your baby at all times on a raised changing surface; babies this age can roll unexpectedly.
source_name: Montessori School of the North Shore

title: Supported push-ups over a towel roll
summary: Raise your baby's chest on a folded towel so it is easier to push up through straight arms.
how_to: Fold a blanket or towel and place it under your baby's chest, about 4 to 6 inches high, with their hands reaching down to the floor. Put a mirror or book in front to keep their head up. Lower the support gradually as they take more weight on their arms.
materials: folded blanket, towel or firm pillow
safety_notes: Supervise tummy time at all times and stop when your baby tires or fusses. Keep the support firm so your baby's face can't sink into it.

title: Prop sitting with a nursing pillow
summary: Practise sitting with hands on the floor for balance, with a nursing pillow for support.
how_to: Sit your baby on the floor with a nursing pillow wrapped around their front so they lean forward on their hands. Put something to look at in front of them rather than something to grab, since both hands are needed for balance. Keep sessions to a few minutes; floor time on back and tummy still builds most of the strength.
safety_notes: Stay within arm's reach; babies tip over easily at this stage. Limit baby seats and propped sitting to short periods.

title: Roll across the midline
summary: Move a toy slowly across your baby's body so they reach over and start to roll.
how_to: Lay your baby on their back and hold a crinkly or noisy toy on one side. Slowly move it across their body to the other side. They will reach across the middle and may roll onto their side or tummy to follow it.
safety_notes: Play on the floor, never on a bed or changing table, now that your baby is rolling.

title: Interlocking discs
summary: Two wooden discs joined at right angles are easy to grab, turn and mouth, and later pass hand to hand.
how_to: Offer the interlocking discs during floor time, either placed in your baby's hand or just within reach. Let them grasp, twist and mouth the discs. Over the coming weeks you may see them pass the discs from one hand to the other.
safety_notes: Use a glued set that cannot come apart, sized too big to fit in the mouth. Supervise mouthing.

title: Rainbow ribbon tactile mobile
summary: Progression from the month 4 bell on a ribbon: ribbons hung from a hoop give your baby lots of fabric to grab, pull down and mouth.
how_to: Tie loops of ribbon around an embroidery hoop until it is covered and hang it on elastic over the movement mat. Lay your baby underneath so they can reach up, grab ribbons and pull them toward their mouth. The elastic lets the mobile come down to them and spring back.
safety_notes: Long ribbons are a strangulation risk: keep them short, check knots, and only use the mobile while you are in the room. Take it down when not supervised.

title: Pull off the sock
summary: A half-on sock tempts your baby to reach for their feet and pull it off.
how_to: With your baby on their back, slide a brightly coloured sock partway onto one foot. Lift their feet toward their face if they need help seeing it. Let them grab with one or both hands and tug the sock off, then put it back for another go.
materials: colourful baby sock or rattle sock

title: Raspberry and squeal echo
summary: When your baby babbles, squeals or blows a raspberry, copy it back and add a new sound.
how_to: Get face to face as soon as your baby vocalises. Copy their sound ('ahhh', a squeal or a raspberry), then try a new one like 'baaa' or 'maaa'. Pause a few seconds for their reply and see how many turns you can take.

title: Shake, shake, shake
summary: Pair a rattle with simple repeated words and big facial expressions.
how_to: Hold your baby on your lap facing you. Shake a rattle and say 'Shake, shake, shake.' When they look at it, make an excited face, shake again and repeat the words. Then pause and let your baby answer with sounds or a reach.

title: House tour
summary: Carry your baby around the house and talk slowly about what you see, hear and touch.
how_to: Pick up your baby and walk through an everyday task: opening the door, running the tap, unloading the dryer. Speak slowly so they can hear the gaps between words ('I'm opening the door... feel the breeze?'). Answer whenever they make a sound back.
safety_notes: Check water temperature before putting fingers under the tap, and keep your baby away from hot appliances.

title: Kick, kick, kick turn-taking
summary: A back-and-forth kicking game teaches your baby that their cues keep the play going.
how_to: Lay your baby on their back. Smile, make eye contact and say 'kick, kick, kick' as you help them kick. Pause and watch for a signal to continue, like eye contact, kicking or a sound, then respond with more play.

title: Peekaboo with a cloth
summary: Hide your face behind a light cloth and pop out again; the surprise of your return gets laughs.
how_to: Hold a light scarf or cloth in front of your face. After a moment, peek out and say 'Here I am!' Repeat while your baby is enjoying it, and let them grab and pull the cloth too.
safety_notes: Use a breathable cloth, don't lay it over your baby's face, and put it away after play.

title: Reflective treasures
summary: Explore mirrors, shiny spoons and foil so your baby meets the 'other baby' and sees light bounce around.
how_to: Set out a stand-up baby mirror, a shiny spoon, a measuring bowl and a tub covered in foil. Lie or sit with your baby and let them look, touch and taste. Join any game they invent with their reflection, such as peekaboo or sticking out a tongue.
safety_notes: Use only shatter-resistant mirrors. Watch that foil isn't torn off and mouthed.

title: Mouthing basket rotation
summary: Offer a few small rattles and teethers your baby can grab and bring to the mouth, and rotate them.
how_to: Choose two or three easy-grip items such as grasping beads, a soft teether, a squishy rattle or a small rubber ball. Put them within reach on the movement mat. When interest drops, swap one item for a different texture or sound.
safety_notes: Pick items too large to fit fully in the mouth with no detachable parts. Wash teethers often.

title: Rolling sensory bottle
summary: A sealed bottle of coloured water and oil sloshes as it rolls, giving your baby something to watch and chase.
how_to: Fill a clear plastic bottle two-thirds with water, add a drop of blue food colouring and top it up with baby oil. Glue the lid on. Roll it slowly in front of your baby during tummy time or let them hold and turn it.
safety_notes: Glue the lid shut and check it before each use; the contents should never reach your baby's mouth.

title: Just out of reach
summary: Place a favourite toy slightly beyond reach so your baby works to get it.
how_to: During tummy time, put a toy just past your baby's fingertips. Let them stretch and wiggle toward it for a few tries. Then nudge it closer and let them have it so the effort pays off.
safety_notes: Don't tease by moving the toy away; give it to your baby before frustration builds.

title: Shady blanket outdoors
summary: Spread a blanket on the grass in the shade for floor time, songs and short board books outside.
how_to: Lay a blanket in a shady spot and put your baby on their back or tummy. Let them watch the leaves and sky, feel the breeze, and touch the grass at the edge. Read a short board book or sing a familiar song.
safety_notes: Keep your baby in the shade with a sun hat (sunscreen isn't generally recommended under 6 months), dress in layers, and avoid very hot days.

title: Starry cardboard box
summary: String lights poked through a big box make a soft 'night sky' for your baby to gaze at.
how_to: Poke holes in the sides of a cardboard box big enough to lay your baby in. Push string lights through from the outside and plug them in. Lay your baby inside and dim the room lights.
safety_notes: Keep cords and bulbs on the outside of the box and out of reach. Never leave your baby alone with it, and unplug the lights after play.

title: Tummy time book corner
summary: Stand a board book in front of your baby during tummy time and read a page or two.
how_to: Open a board book with bright colours or real photos and stand it in front of your baby during tummy time. Read a page or just name the pictures. Keep it short and come back to books several times a day.
materials: board books with bright pictures or photos
safety_notes: Supervise tummy time at all times and stop when your baby tires or fusses.

title: Laundry basket sleigh ride
summary: Pull your baby around the room in a basket so they practise balancing, turning and leaning while seated.
how_to: Sit your baby in a laundry basket or sturdy box, with pillows or blankets around them if they need support. Pull it slowly around the room and narrate what you pass. Change speed and direction gently so they adjust their balance.
materials: laundry basket or sturdy cardboard box
safety_notes: Go slowly on a flat floor, keep away from stairs and furniture edges, and stay close enough to steady the basket.

title: Chase the interlocking discs
summary: Progression from month 5: a light tap makes the discs wobble a short way off, so your baby stretches, pivots or rolls to get them back.
how_to: Place the interlocking discs just beyond your baby's reach during floor time, or tap them so they wobble away. The slow movement keeps the toy close enough to catch. Let your baby work to reach it rather than handing it back right away.
safety_notes: Clear the floor of small objects and keep the play space away from stairs now that your baby is moving more.

title: Reach-and-twist sitting
summary: Progression from month 5 prop sitting: toys placed low and to the sides teach a wobbly sitter to balance while reaching.
how_to: Sit behind your baby with your legs in a V, or wrap a nursing pillow around their hips. Place toys below chest level, first in front, then to the sides, so they turn and reach. As balance improves, spread toys further around them.
materials: nursing pillow or your legs as a boundary
safety_notes: Stay within arm's reach and keep soft surfaces around your baby; they don't yet catch themselves when they tip.

title: Tissue box pull
summary: Pulling fabric 'tissues' out of a box on its side builds grasp, reach and shoulder strength.
how_to: Lay a tissue box on its side in front of your baby during tummy time, filled with washable fabric squares or Magic Tissues. Show them how one comes out, then let them pull. When this gets easy, move the box a little further away so they stretch and push off to reach it.
materials: empty tissue box or Lovevery Magic Tissue Box
safety_notes: Don't use real tissues or wipes, which can cause choking when soggy. Use fabric pieces and supervise.

title: Real kitchen tools
summary: Let your baby handle a bowl, whisk, spatula and measuring spoons to build finger strength and hand-eye coordination.
how_to: Place a few baby-safe kitchen tools within reach during tummy time or supported sitting. Let your baby grab, mouth and bang them. Sit with them and name each tool and show what it does.
safety_notes: Supervise throughout, check for sharp edges or loose parts, and put the tools away after play.

title: Two-handed grab across the middle
summary: Hold a larger object in front of your sitting baby, then off to one side, so they reach with both hands across the middle.
how_to: Sit your baby in front of you, supported by your body or pillows. Hold a large soft book or toy right in front of them. Once they grab it with both hands, offer it a little to one side next time so they have to cross the midline.
materials: soft cloth book or large soft toy
safety_notes: Keep your baby supported so reaching doesn't tip them over.

title: Babble back, but shorter
summary: Progression from month 5's sound echo: answer your baby's babble chains with short double sounds like 'baba' and real words like 'bye-bye'.
how_to: When your baby babbles 'bababababa', smile and reply 'baba'. Slip real double-consonant words into the day, like 'bye-bye' when the dog goes out. Respond to babbling straight away as if it's real conversation ('Oh really?').

title: Name game
summary: Use your baby's name often and warmly so they start to turn when they hear it.
how_to: Say your baby's name throughout the day in a high, warm voice: at meals, during peekaboo ('Where's Emilia? There she is!'), on walks. Use the same name each time and ask other caregivers to do the same. Watch for a pause, a look or a smile when they hear it.

title: Mirror face tour
summary: Name and touch the parts of your baby's face while they watch in a mirror.
how_to: Lie next to your baby on their tummy in front of a floor mirror. While they look at their reflection, touch and name each part: 'This is your nose. Can you feel my finger on your nose?' Go slowly and pause for their looks and coos before the next one.
safety_notes: Use a shatter-resistant mirror. Supervise tummy time at all times and stop when your baby tires or fusses.

title: Hello and goodbye flap book
summary: Lift and drop fabric flaps over baby faces in a book, saying 'hello' and 'goodbye', to help with early separation feelings.
how_to: Tape fabric pieces to the top of a few pages in a book of baby faces so they make flaps. Lift a flap and say 'hello!', then drop it and say 'goodbye'. Repeat the pattern so your baby sees that goodbye is followed by hello again.
safety_notes: Check that the tape and fabric are secure so they don't come off in your baby's mouth.

title: Your turn, my turn
summary: Take turns pulling fabric pieces out of a box to practise shared attention and focus.
how_to: Sit with your baby and a box of fabric squares. Pull one out yourself, then say 'Your turn' and help them reach. Narrate as you go ('It's a yellow one! You're working hard') and keep swapping turns while they're interested.
materials: tissue box with fabric squares, or Lovevery Magic Tissue Box
safety_notes: Use fabric, not real tissues or wipes.

title: Movement-area mirror
summary: Progression from month 5's reflective play: a low mirror by the play mat lets your baby watch themselves and look around the room, then back at you.
how_to: Lean or mount a shatter-resistant mirror low against the wall beside your baby's movement mat. Let your baby discover it during free floor time. Notice when they look at you in the mirror and then turn to find you, and smile back.
safety_notes: Secure the mirror so it can't tip, use shatter-resistant or acrylic, and keep it away from the sleep space.

title: Where did the ball go?
summary: Partly hide a familiar toy under a cloth to start building object permanence.
how_to: Let your baby watch as you cover part of a favourite ball or toy with a cloth. Ask 'Where is the ball?' and see if they reach for it. If not, lift the cloth to show the rest ('There it is!') and try again.

title: Fabric texture basket
summary: A basket of three different fabric squares invites long, focused exploration by touch and mouth.
how_to: Put three fabric squares in a basket, for example soft terry cloth, cotton gingham and a sheer rough fabric. Place it on a low shelf or the mat near your baby. Let them pull out, mouth, toss and pick up the fabrics without directing them.
safety_notes: Use squares big enough not to be stuffed into the mouth, with no loose threads. Wash them often.

title: Sound block in and out
summary: Take a sound block out of its basket and put it back, saying 'in' and 'out', or roll a rattling cylinder away to retrieve.
how_to: Put a wooden sound block in a small basket. Show your baby: take it out, say 'out', put it back, say 'in'. Let them shake, mouth and explore. With a cylinder-shaped sound block, roll it a short way off to encourage movement, then return it to the basket.
materials: wooden sound block or cylinder rattle
safety_notes: Choose a sealed, well-made sound block with no parts that can come loose.

title: Outdoor scent tour
summary: Carry your baby outside to sniff flowers, pine needles and cut grass while you name each smell.
how_to: Walk outside and look for things to smell. Bring your baby close, show them how to sniff, and describe the scent and where it comes from ('This is a rose. It smells sweet'). Let them touch safe leaves or bark too.
safety_notes: Avoid plants that are toxic, thorny or sprayed with chemicals, and keep leaves and petals out of the mouth. Use shade and a sun hat.

title: First meals at a weaning table
summary: Once your baby shows readiness for solids, offer first foods at a small, sturdy table and chair with a real small spoon and cup.
how_to: Set up a low, heavy table and supportive chair so your baby's feet rest flat on the floor. Sit facing them on a low stool and offer a few first foods with a small real spoon and cup. Let them explore and stop when they turn away or close their lips.
safety_notes: Start solids only when your baby can sit upright with little help and shows interest; check with your pediatrician first. Serve soft, mashable foods, never leave your baby alone while eating, and introduce common allergens one at a time as advised by your doctor.
source_name: Montessori School of the North Shore

title: Sound basket of real instruments
summary: Keep a few light wooden and metal shakers and bells in a corner of the play space for your baby to shake, roll and compare.
how_to: Fill a small basket with two or three light instruments: jingle bells, a soft shaker, a wooden rattle. Place it where your baby plays. Let them hold, roll and shake them, noticing the different sounds and the warm wood versus cool metal.
safety_notes: Choose sturdy baby instruments with no small detachable parts; bells must be fixed to a handle or strap.

title: Reach-around sitting circle
summary: Toys placed all around a newly independent sitter get them twisting and reaching while keeping their balance.
how_to: Once your baby sits on their own, set 4-5 toys in a circle around them, some to the side and some just behind. Put one toy on the floor at a diagonal, just barely out of reach, so they have to lean with one arm and come back up. Stay within arm's reach while they wobble.
safety_notes: Sitting babies still tip over. Clear hard objects from behind them and keep a pillow or your legs nearby to soften falls.

title: Ball just out of reach
summary: A ball rolled just beyond reach during tummy time motivates belly-scooting forward.
how_to: Dress your baby in a short-sleeved onesie with bare legs and put them on a smooth floor, not a rug. Roll a ball just out of reach while they are on their tummy. Let them get to it, and don't move it farther away as they work toward it.
safety_notes: Use a ball too big to fit in the mouth. Check the floor for small items before tummy time.

title: Rolling-toy ladder for early movers
summary: Offer rolling toys in order from slowest to fastest so a new mover can chase and catch them.
how_to: Start with a bell rattle that rolls away slowly when dropped. When your baby can get to it easily, swap in a ball roller, then a soft ball, then an O-ball, each one rolling a little farther. Watch for the one that is challenging but not frustrating.
safety_notes: Check that rattles and balls are intact and too large to choke on. Supervise mouthing.

title: Metal treasure basket
summary: A small basket of safe metal kitchen objects to grasp, pass between hands, bang, and mouth.
how_to: Fill a low basket with a few metal objects: a small whisk, a baby spoon, a metal measuring spoon, a small metal bowl, a jar lid. Set it in front of your sitting baby and let them explore however they like. Rotate the items every few days or when interest drops.
safety_notes: Only include items too large to swallow, with no sharp edges or loose parts. Watch closely with long-handled items like whisks and spoons.

title: Pull-apart nesting cups
summary: Two small nesting cups give a baby something to grip with both hands and pull apart.
how_to: Nest the two smallest stacking cups together and hand them to your baby. Let them work at pulling them apart, mouthing and passing each cup hand to hand. Don't expect them to put the cups back together yet; you can show how once in a while.
safety_notes: Check cups for cracks or sharp edges.

title: Blanket in a bowl
summary: Stuff a small blanket into a bowl and let your baby work both hands to pull it out.
how_to: While your baby watches, stuff a small blanket or scarf into a large bowl or basket. Set it in front of them and see if they can grab and pull it out, using both hands. Stuff it back and repeat while they stay interested.
safety_notes: Supervise with blankets and fabric; put them away after play and keep them out of sleep spaces.

title: Babble back-and-forth
summary: Copy your baby's babbles, add one new sound, and pause so they can take a turn.
how_to: Get face to face when your baby babbles or squeals. Repeat their sound, then add a new one: 'bababa' becomes 'baba, mama.' Wait a few seconds for a reply and see how many turns you can trade.

title: "Up?" before lifting
summary: Say 'Up?' and hold your arms out for a moment before you pick your baby up, so they learn to signal back.
how_to: Before each pick-up, kneel in front of your baby, hold out your arms, and say 'Up?' in a clear, happy voice. Wait a beat to see if they reach or lift their arms, then lift them and say 'Up!' Repeat at every pick-up through the day.

title: Name-and-peekaboo game
summary: Use your baby's name often, including in peekaboo, so they connect it with themselves and with warm attention.
how_to: Use the same name every time and say it in a bright, high voice at meals and diaper changes. Play peekaboo with it: hide your face and ask 'Where's Mia?', then reveal 'There she is!' Ask other caregivers to use the same name.

title: Short goodbye ritual
summary: A quick, predictable goodbye helps your baby learn that you leave and come back.
how_to: Don't sneak out. Get your baby's attention, smile, hug or kiss them, say 'I love you, goodbye,' tell them when you'll be back, and go. Keep it short and calm. When you return, greet them warmly and say how happy you are to see them.

title: Copy my face
summary: Mirror your baby's facial expressions and pause, so they see faces as part of a conversation.
how_to: Watch your baby's face during calm play. When they make an expression (surprise, a frown, a big smile), copy it back with a little exaggeration. Pause and see what they do next; keep the exchange going.

title: Hide it under a clear cup
summary: Cover a toy or snack with a clear cup so your baby can still see it and learns to lift the cover.
how_to: Show your baby a favorite toy, then cover it with an upside-down clear cup while they watch. If they get stuck, put your hand over theirs and lift the cup together. Once they get it, switch to an opaque cover like a small box or cloth.
safety_notes: If you use food, choose a dissolvable puff and stay with your baby.

title: Copy-the-bang game
summary: Take a movement your baby already does, like banging a toy, and turn it into a back-and-forth imitation game.
how_to: Notice what your baby does with toys, such as banging or waving. Later, bang a rattle on the table or wave a scarf yourself, then hand it over and invite them to copy. If needed, put your hand over theirs; take turns a few times.

title: Sound hide-and-seek
summary: Shake a sealed sound bottle out of sight and let your baby turn and search for the sound.
how_to: Fill a few small bottles with different things (rice, a bell, pebbles) and glue or tape the lids shut. Shake one in front of your baby and say 'loud' or 'soft'. Then shake it behind your back or under a scarf and see if they turn or reach to find it.
safety_notes: Seal lids with glue or tape so they cannot open; check seals before each use and supervise mouthing.

title: A place at the family table
summary: Seat your baby at the family table with their own small place setting during meals.
how_to: Pull a high chair up to the family table at mealtimes. When you can, set a small mat, plate, spoon, and cup for your baby. Let them watch, smell, and taste while everyone eats and talks together.
safety_notes: Offer only foods prepared to a safe texture and size for your baby; keep them seated upright and supervised while eating.

title: Shakers and a drum
summary: Simple instruments like egg shakers, bells, and a small drum connect your baby's movement to sound.
how_to: Put an egg shaker, a set of jingle bells, and a small drum in a basket. Show how each makes a sound, then let your baby shake and bang. Put on a song and move along with them.
safety_notes: Choose instruments with no small loose parts; babies will mouth them.

title: Follow-the-baby reading
summary: Page through simple board books with your baby and let them set the pace.
how_to: Sit together with a board book. You don't need to read every word; point and talk about the pictures. Stop when your baby wiggles away, and keep reading aloud even if they move around.

title: Low pull-up stool
summary: A sturdy footstool or firm cushion in the play area gives your baby a safe first thing to pull up on.
how_to: Put a sturdy, low footstool, firm floor cushion, or small heavy chair in your baby's movement area. Let them discover it: climbing on it, pulling to their knees, and later to their feet. Don't lift them into standing; let every move be their own.
materials: sturdy low footstool or firm cushion
safety_notes: Use furniture that cannot tip or slide when pulled on. Pad hard floors around it and stay nearby while your baby pulls up.

title: Blanket ride
summary: Pull your seated baby slowly across the floor on a blanket to challenge their sitting balance.
how_to: Sit your baby in the middle of a blanket on a smooth floor. Gently pull the blanket so they glide along, going slowly enough that they can adjust their balance. Try short starts and stops, and stop if they tip.
safety_notes: Go slowly, stay on a clear smooth floor away from furniture edges, and stop if your baby can't stay upright.

title: Pillow mountain
summary: A pile of pillows gives a crawler a soft climb that builds core, shoulder, and hand strength.
how_to: Pile a few firm couch cushions and pillows on the floor. Put your crawling baby at the bottom, maybe with a toy at the top, and let them climb up and over. Rearrange the pile to make new paths.
safety_notes: Never leave your baby alone near pillows; a baby face-down in soft cushions can have trouble breathing. Put the pillows away after play.

title: Tray of soft finger foods
summary: Put a few small, soft food pieces on the high chair tray and let your baby rake, grab, and squish them.
how_to: Place a few pieces of O-shaped cereal or soft food (banana, avocado, pancake) on the tray. Let your baby try different grasps: raking, grabbing, pinching. If they can't get a piece to their mouth, let them keep trying instead of doing it for them.
materials: soft banana, avocado, or pancake pieces
safety_notes: Choking risk: keep pieces no bigger than half an inch, soft enough to mash, and only offer food when your baby is seated upright and you are right there.

title: Egg and cup
summary: A wooden egg and cup give a whole-hand grip and an early 'in and out' challenge.
how_to: Sit with your baby and slowly lift the egg out of the cup and put it back a couple of times. Then hand it over and let them explore freely. Expect them to bang, mouth, and dump it before they place the egg in the cup.
safety_notes: Use an egg too large to fit fully in your baby's mouth.

title: Animal rescue
summary: Tape small animal toys to the floor or wall and let your baby peel the tape to free them.
how_to: Tape a few favorite small animals to a floor, wall, or bathtub side with painter's or washi tape. Show your baby one being pulled free. Let them work on the rest and celebrate each rescue.
safety_notes: Tape and small figures are choking hazards: use figures too big to swallow, watch that tape doesn't go in the mouth, and pick everything up afterward.

title: Name what they babble at
summary: When your baby babbles at something, point to it and say its name clearly.
how_to: Watch where your baby looks when they babble. Point and name it with emphasis: 'Dog! That's a dog.' Copy their babble too, then pause for a reply.

title: "In! Out! Boom!" basket play
summary: Fill a basket for your baby to dump, and name each action with short, lively words.
how_to: Fill a basket with balls, blocks, balled-up socks, and a scarf. Let your baby dump it all out, then refill it and repeat. Each time something goes in say 'In! In!', and when it comes out say 'Out! Boom!'
safety_notes: Choose objects too large to swallow and without strings or cords.

title: Lap-bounce rhymes
summary: Bouncing rhymes like 'Trot, Trot to Boston' give your baby the rhythm and patterns of speech.
how_to: Sit your baby on your knees facing you, holding them securely under the arms. Bounce gently in time to 'Trot, trot to Boston, trot, trot to Lynn' and give a small, safe dip on 'fall in!' Repeat the same rhymes often so they learn what comes next.
safety_notes: Hold your baby firmly under the arms; keep bounces and dips gentle, with no shaking.

title: Slow warm-up with visitors
summary: Let your baby warm up to guests at their own pace instead of passing them straight into new arms.
how_to: Tell visitors ahead of time that your baby may need a while. Greet calmly, and ask guests to speak softly, move slowly, and wait for a sign of comfort (a smile, raised arms, a reach) before touching or holding. If your baby is upset, name the feeling: 'You don't know her yet, and that feels scary.'

title: Goodbye toolkit for the caregiver
summary: Builds on the short goodbye: give the caregiver a special toy, song, or photo album to use as you leave.
how_to: Keep your usual short goodbye. Add one thing that only comes out when you leave: a special toy, a 'goodbye song', or a photo album of you and your baby. The caregiver can also wave with your baby from the window, then point out things outside.

title: Name the scary thing
summary: When a sudden sound or sight startles your baby, hold them, name the feeling, and explain what happened.
how_to: If the blender, vacuum, or a dog scares your baby, pick them up and hold them close until they calm. Say what happened: 'That was a loud sound. Are you feeling scared? It was the vacuum.' Avoid the trigger for now if you can; these fears usually pass.

title: Object permanence box
summary: A ball dropped into a hole disappears, then rolls back out into a tray.
how_to: Bring out the box once your baby starts dropping things and looking for them. Slowly drop the ball in a couple of times so they see it vanish and come back. Expect several weeks of just playing with the ball before they try the hole.
materials: object permanence box with ball (or DIY box with ramp and tray)
safety_notes: Use a ball that is too big to be a choking hazard.

title: High chair drop zone
summary: Give your baby a box to drop things into from the high chair so they can watch where things fall.
how_to: Put a cardboard box on the floor below the high chair. Hand your baby soft things (felt balls, tissues) and hard things (large kitchen spoons, plastic measuring cups) to drop in. Once they get it, move the box and show them how to aim.
safety_notes: Make sure the high chair harness is buckled and objects are too large to swallow.

title: Bang the blocks
summary: Help your baby bang two blocks together, then knock down small towers you build.
how_to: Give your baby only 3-4 blocks. Put your hands over theirs and bang two blocks together, maybe in a rhythm, then see if they copy you. Build a small tower and let them knock it down: 'Boom!'
safety_notes: Use blocks too large to choke on, with smooth edges.

title: Water tray on the floor
summary: A sheet pan with a little water on a towel lets your baby splash and crawl through water play.
how_to: Lay a towel on the kitchen floor and set a sheet pan on it with just a couple of ounces of water, not enough to cover a face. Let your baby splash, pat, and crawl over it. Stay right there the whole time.
safety_notes: Drowning risk: never leave your baby alone with any amount of water, use only a shallow layer, and empty it right after play.

title: Little helper chores
summary: Include your baby in everyday chores with a safe job to hold or try.
how_to: While folding laundry, hand them a sock and name each piece of clothing. Show how to wipe the floor with a wet washcloth and let them have a turn. Give them pots, pans, and spoons to bang while you cook, or help them water a plant with a small can.
safety_notes: Keep your baby away from the stove, hot food, and cleaning products. Supervise around water.

title: Smelling jars
summary: Small sealed jars with herbs, citrus peel, or a cinnamon stick let your baby explore smells.
how_to: Put fresh herbs, a strip of citrus peel, or a cinnamon stick into small shaker jars and close them tightly. Hold one near your baby's nose, sniff it yourself to show how, and name the smell. Leave a couple in a basket on their shelf.
materials: small shaker jars with secure lids
safety_notes: Lids must be secure so contents can't be eaten. Avoid essential oils near the face and replace contents when they dry out.

title: Cruise-friendly living room
summary: Arrange sturdy furniture and toys so a baby who pulls up has reasons to stand and side-step.
how_to: Take the seat cushions off the couch and put books or toys on the frame, at a height your baby reaches once standing. Move a sturdy chair or ottoman beside the couch so they can step from one to the other. Place a toy just out of reach along the surface and move it a bit farther as they gain confidence.
safety_notes: Pad or cover sharp furniture corners, anchor anything that could tip, and check for spots where your baby could fall onto hard edges.

title: Standing to sitting practice
summary: Help a baby who gets 'stuck' standing learn to lower back down to sitting.
how_to: Sit cross-legged in front of a coffee table or cushion-free couch with a toy on top so your baby pulls up. After a minute or two, gently guide their hips down into your lap, giving as little help as possible. Later, offer toys at knee height so they mini-squat while holding on, then at floor level for a full squat.
safety_notes: Use stable furniture that won't tip; stay close and let your baby try their own way down before you step in.

title: Pull-up bar with mirror
summary: Builds on the low pull-up stool: a wall-mounted bar at your baby's height lets them pull up and cruise at their own pace.
how_to: Mount a wooden bar (a dowel or closet rod on brackets) securely into wall studs, with a shatter-proof mirror behind it. Set the height so your baby can grab it from sitting and cruise with hands about chest height. Let them use it freely; don't pull them up or walk them along it.
safety_notes: Screw the bar into studs and test it with your own weight. Use acrylic or safety mirror, and keep a soft rug below.

title: Peg and cup
summary: A progression from the egg and cup: a narrower peg makes your baby use fingers instead of the whole hand.
how_to: Show your baby how to lift the wooden peg out of its cup and drop it back in, slowly, once or twice. Then let them try. Expect lots of mouthing and missed attempts at first.
safety_notes: Use a peg too large to choke on and check that the wood is smooth and unsplintered.

title: Open cup sips
summary: Offer a little water in a small open cup at seated meals so your baby learns to tilt and sip.
how_to: At seated meals with finger foods, pour no more than an inch of water into a small, heavy open cup. Drink from your own cup to show how, then hold theirs steady while they bring it to their mouth with two hands. Spills, pouring, and banging are part of learning.
materials: small open cup or small heavy glass
safety_notes: Keep water to about an inch and no more than about 4 ounces a day; breast milk or formula stays the main drink. If using glass, choose a small thick one and supervise.

title: Unwrap a surprise
summary: Loosely wrap a favorite toy in paper and ribbon for your baby to tear open.
how_to: Wrap a familiar toy, ideally one that makes a sound, loosely in bright paper with a ribbon. Hand it to your baby and let them crinkle, pull, and tear. If they get stuck, poke a small hole to get them started.
safety_notes: Tape, ribbon, and paper bits are choking hazards. Stay with your baby, don't let them mouth these, and clear them away after.

title: Bye-bye waves
summary: Wave hello and goodbye to your baby throughout the day and help them wave back.
how_to: Gently hold your baby's hand and wave it as you say 'Hi!' or 'Bye-bye!' Wave every time you leave a room or put them down for a nap. Wave to a stuffed animal during peekaboo or in a mirror, and always wave back when your baby waves.

title: "That's Mama!"
summary: When your baby babbles 'mama' or 'dada', point to that person and name them so the sound starts to carry meaning.
how_to: When you hear 'mamama' or 'dadada', point to the parent and say 'Yes, that's Mama!' Repeat your baby's babbles back to them. During peekaboo, say a single 'Boo!' or 'Ba!' when you reveal yourself to model one-syllable sounds.

title: Bubble, ball, pour: bath words
summary: Use bath time to repeat words that start with the early sounds b, m, and p.
how_to: Face your baby in the bath and repeat words like bubble, ball, boat, more, pour, and pop as you play: 'Look, the b-b-bubble pops!' Name body parts as you wash them, and say action words like scoop and splash as they happen.
safety_notes: Stay within arm's reach every second; babies can drown in an inch of water. Check water temperature first.

title: Pat-a-cake and clapping songs
summary: Clapping and rhyming games like Pat-a-Cake and Open Shut Them invite your baby into turn-taking play.
how_to: Sit facing your baby and sing 'Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake, baker's man', clapping your hands and then gently clapping theirs. Try 'Open Shut Them' and 'This Little Piggy' too. Repeat the same few songs daily so your baby can anticipate and join in.

title: Pull-it-off peekaboo
summary: Your baby takes the active role in peekaboo by pulling the blanket off your head.
how_to: Cover your head with a light blanket and ask 'Where am I?' Lean toward your baby so they can grab it and pull it off, then react with a big 'Here I am!' Swap roles by gently covering their head for a second.
safety_notes: Use a light, breathable cloth and only cover your baby's head for a second or two.

title: Limits by redirection
summary: Set limits for a mobile baby by changing the space first, then modeling and redirecting, saving 'stop' for danger.
how_to: Remove or put away things your baby shouldn't handle. If something must stay, show the right way with slow, exaggerated movements. If they still reach for it, say calmly 'Glasses stay on the shelf. Let's play with your toys,' and move them to something they can use. Save a firm 'Stop!' for real danger.
materials: safe alternative toys or a treasure basket
safety_notes: Lock away or remove hazards rather than relying on words; babies this age can't reliably follow a limit.

title: Imbucare box
summary: The next step after the object permanence box: your baby posts an object through a hole and reaches in or around to find it.
how_to: Use a store-bought imbucare box or make one: cut a hole in a container lid and gather a few child-safe objects like large corks or cardboard discs. Show your baby how to drop one in, saying 'open', 'shut', and 'gone', then let them try and find it again.
materials: container with a hole in the lid (or imbucare box)
safety_notes: Objects must be too large to fit in the mouth; smooth the edges of any cut holes.

title: Muffin tin balls
summary: A muffin tin full of balls gives 12 little containers for taking out and, eventually, putting back.
