how_to: Prop a board or large book on a cushion to make a ramp. Gather a ball, a block, and a peg and let your toddler choose which to try first, next, and last. Narrate the result: "The ball rolled fast because it's round."
safety_notes: Use objects too large to swallow.

title: Color filter mixing
summary: Your toddler layers circles of colored light filter to watch colors change.
how_to: Cut colored lighting gels or cellophane into circles and set them on a tray. Show once how two colors overlap to make a new one, then let your toddler explore freely. Give color words for what they discover rather than quizzing them.
safety_notes: Cellophane can be a suffocation hazard if mouthed; supervise.

title: Sort pom poms by color
summary: Your toddler sorts pom poms by color into a muffin tin or egg carton.
how_to: Put a handful of pom poms in two or three colors in a bowl next to a muffin tin. Place one of each color in its own cup as a guide. Let your toddler sort with fingers or child tweezers; sort by size too if you have big and small ones.
safety_notes: Pom poms are a choking hazard; stay within reach.

title: Laundry helper
summary: Your toddler helps carry, load, and sort laundry.
how_to: Ask your toddler to carry a small item to the basket while you carry the rest, move clothes from washer to dryer, or press the start button. Keep each job to one or two steps and thank them for helping the family.
safety_notes: Keep detergent pods out of reach; supervise around machine doors.

title: Bath squeeze toys
summary: Add a squeeze bottle, sponge, and turkey baster to the bath and name how each one feels.
how_to: Put a clean squeeze bottle, a sponge, and a baster in the bath. As your toddler squeezes and squirts, describe it: "The sponge is squishy," "The bottle is slippery."
safety_notes: Stay within arm's reach at all times; toddlers can drown in less than an inch of water.

title: Nature treasure basket
summary: Your toddler explores a basket of natural materials collected outside, comparing textures, shapes, and weights.
how_to: Collect a few large natural items together, such as pinecones, smooth stones, bark, and leaves. Put a few in a shallow basket and let your toddler handle them freely. Watch what interests them and add similar items next time.
safety_notes: Choose items too big to swallow and avoid toxic plants and berries.

title: Ramps, bridges, and stepping stones
summary: At the playground, your toddler tackles slopes, wobbly bridges, and stepping stones while holding your hand.
how_to: Let your toddler walk up and down a ramp and across a bridge, gently bouncing in place to feel their weight shift. Hold hands across stepping stones or a low balance beam. Walking on gravel, sand, and woodchips is a balance challenge too.
safety_notes: Stay within reach on raised equipment; don't slide with your toddler on your lap.

title: Kick-and-toss ball bins
summary: Your toddler kicks and throws balls of different sizes into big bins, alone or with a playmate.
how_to: Gather a few soft balls in different sizes and put out two laundry baskets or plastic tubs. Show how to kick a ball toward a bin, then try tossing one in. Leave space for two children to play at once.
safety_notes: Use soft balls and keep the area clear of breakables.

title: Neighborhood walk on foot
summary: Skip the stroller for 20 minutes and let your toddler walk, run, and climb wherever their curiosity leads.
how_to: Head out from your door on foot with no destination. Let your toddler set the pace, run on safe paths, step up curbs, and climb over tree roots. If they're used to the stroller, start with a "last-block walk" at the end of an outing.
safety_notes: Toddlers lack impulse control near streets; stay close, or use a fenced park or school field.

title: Matchstick posting
summary: Your toddler pushes craft sticks through holes poked in a container lid.
how_to: Poke or cut a few holes in the soft plastic lid of an oatmeal or coffee container. Give your toddler a small pile of craft matchsticks and show how to push one through. Open the lid to dump them and start again.
safety_notes: Supervise with sticks; smooth any sharp edges around the holes.

title: Spread your own cracker
summary: Your toddler uses a small spreader to cover a cracker with butter or a soft spread.
how_to: Put a small dab of butter, cream cheese, or hummus in a little dish with a child spreader and a few crackers on a tray. Show slowly how to hold the cracker steady and spread. Only put out as much as you're willing to clean up.
safety_notes: Check for food allergies (e.g. nut butter); seat your toddler while eating.

title: Sticker tray
summary: Your toddler peels simple stickers off a sheet and presses them onto a card.
how_to: Set a sheet of easy-peel stickers and a note card on a small tray. Show how to lift a sticker edge with a fingernail and press it down. Once that's easy, offer smaller stickers.
safety_notes: Stickers can be a choking hazard; supervise.

title: Moo, beep, vroom: sound-and-word play
summary: Play with animals and vehicles while pairing each sound with its name to encourage early word combinations.
how_to: As you play with toy animals or trucks, say the name with the sound: "Cow says moo," "Truck goes beep." Pause for your toddler to copy the sound. When they say one word, add one: "Big truck!"
safety_notes: Avoid small toy parts if your child still mouths toys.

title: Narrate the outing with rich words
summary: During errands and walks, describe what you see in specific, rich words and leave space for your toddler to reply.
how_to: Instead of "big," try "humongous"; instead of "bug," try "monarch butterfly." At the store, narrate: "We need apples. Can you help me put four in the bag?" When your toddler says a word, repeat it and add a little more, then wait for a turn.

title: Language card basket
summary: Look through simple real-photo cards together, naming each picture and letting your toddler point.
how_to: Pick 4–6 picture cards on a theme your toddler likes, such as farm animals or vehicles. Name each one slowly, then ask, "Where's the horse?" and let them point. You can make your own cards by photographing objects in your home.

title: You want bananas, I want strawberries
summary: Show your toddler that people can want different things by choosing differently and saying so.
how_to: At snack time, ask, "Do you want bananas or strawberries?" and wait for an answer. Then pick the other one and point it out: "You want bananas and I want strawberries! Sometimes we want different foods."
safety_notes: Cut fruit into safe, toddler-sized pieces.

title: Explain the scary noise
summary: When something startles your toddler, match their feeling in a calm voice and explain what happened.
how_to: Acknowledge the feeling in a softer version of their tone: "That loud noise surprised you." Explain the cause: "That was the garbage truck. Let's see if we can spot it." Sit close and breathe slowly; once they calm a little, redirect to something similar that soothes them.

title: Real fruit to picture match
summary: Your toddler matches real fruit to its picture card, moving from objects toward pictures.
how_to: Builds on the month-19 figure match with a new set: real fruit. Lay out 3 picture cards and put the matching fruit in a basket. Show how to set the apple on the apple card and name it, then let your toddler try. Keep cards simple, ideally pictures without words.
safety_notes: Watch for biting into whole fruit like grapes; use larger fruits.

title: Block corrals for animals
summary: Your toddler builds a ring of blocks to make a pen for toy animals or a parking lot for cars.
how_to: Start a circle of blocks and put a toy animal inside: "The cow needs a fence." Hand your toddler blocks to finish it, then add more animals or cars. Let them knock it down and rebuild.
safety_notes: Avoid small toy parts for toddlers who mouth objects.

title: Light switch helper
summary: Your toddler moves a light stool to the switch and turns the lights off when leaving a room.
how_to: Give your toddler a lightweight step stool they can move. When you leave a room, ask them to turn off the light, and let them work out how to get the stool there and reach. Add a short phrase: "Light on when we come in, light off when we leave."
safety_notes: Use a wide, stable stool and stay nearby while your toddler climbs it.

title: Dump-and-stir no-bake snack
summary: Make a simple no-bake recipe together, with ingredients measured ahead so your toddler can dump and stir.
how_to: Measure each ingredient into a bowl your toddler can tip easily. Let them dump each one into the mixing bowl and stir. Do the sticky scraping yourself and enjoy the snack together.
safety_notes: Check for allergies; keep knives and hot appliances out of reach.

title: Splash and pour water bin
summary: Give your toddler's urge to throw a safe outlet: tossing cups and toys into water and pouring it out again.
how_to: Set a shallow bin or baby pool outside with plastic cups and small floating toys. Let your toddler toss things in to make splashes and pour water out with a cup or small pitcher. Indoors, use a water tray on towels.
safety_notes: Supervise at all times; toddlers can drown in less than an inch of water. Empty the bin after play.

title: Clay as a whole-body discovery
summary: Your toddler meets a large slab of natural clay for the first time with hands, feet, and whole body.
how_to: Cover the floor with a plastic sheet and put down a big block of soft natural clay. Let your toddler explore it however they want: patting, poking, standing on it, or just watching. Note what they do and take photos to look back on together.
safety_notes: Clay is not food; supervise mouthing and wash hands afterward.

title: Balloon paddle tennis
summary: Bat a balloon back and forth with paper-plate paddles, running and reaching to keep it in the air.
how_to: Tape a craft stick to a paper plate to make a paddle and blow up a balloon. Pass the balloon back and forth, or each try to keep one in the air. With three people, play monkey in the middle so your toddler runs to grab it.
safety_notes: Popped or uninflated balloons are a serious choking hazard; adults inflate, supervise closely, and throw away pieces at once.

title: Maximum-effort carrying
summary: Your toddler carries and moves heavy, bulky things like couch cushions, a small bucket of water, or books up the stairs.
how_to: Offer heavy-work jobs: carrying couch cushions across a room, moving a loaded wagon, or carrying a light bag up the stairs with you. Toddlers often seek this kind of full-body effort, so let them repeat it.
safety_notes: Stay beside your toddler on stairs; keep loads small enough to see over. Supervise any bucket of water.

title: Animal moves
summary: Stomp like a dinosaur, creep like a spider, hop like a bunny, and waddle like a duck.
how_to: Call out an animal and show its move, then let your toddler copy. Mix big stomps, low creeps, and little hops. Bunny hops that look like squats still build strength.
safety_notes: Clear a space free of sharp corners.

title: Tweezer transfer with felt stars
summary: Your toddler uses toddler tweezers to move felt stars or pom poms from one cup to another.
how_to: Progresses from month-19 spooning to a tool that needs a pinch. Put felt stars, pom poms, or penne pasta in one cup and an empty cup beside it. Show how to squeeze the tweezers, pick one up, and drop it in. Fingers are fine if tweezers frustrate them.
materials: toddler tweezers (e.g. Transfer Tweezers & Felt Stars, Lovevery Companion kit)
felt stars, pom poms, or penne pasta
safety_notes: Small items are choking hazards; supervise and put them away after play.

title: Bead threading on a pipe cleaner
summary: Your toddler threads large beads onto a pipe cleaner, then slides them off and starts again.
how_to: Give a pipe cleaner (stiff enough to need no needle) and a small number of large beads so they can finish. Show how to hold the pipe cleaner in one hand and push a bead on with the other. Later, move to smaller beads and a stringing cord with a stiff tip.
materials: pipe cleaner or thick cord with a stiff tip
safety_notes: Beads are a choking hazard and cords a strangulation risk; supervise and store out of reach.

title: Cereal shaker
summary: Your toddler drops O-shaped cereal one piece at a time into the small opening of a carton, then shakes it.
how_to: Rinse and dry a milk carton or small bottle. Show your toddler how to pinch one cereal O and drop it through the opening. When they're done, screw on the lid together and shake their new instrument.
materials: empty carton or bottle with small opening and lid
safety_notes: Supervise; cereal is a minor choking risk for some toddlers.

title: Light on, light off
summary: Model short two-word phrases at key moments so your toddler can start copying them.
how_to: Say "Light on" when you flip the switch and "Light off" when you turn it off. End longer sentences with the pair: "Do you want more to eat? More avocado?" When your toddler says one word, add one: "Dog!" "Big dog!" Choose phrases that get their needs met, like "open door" or "shoes on."

title: Touch your nose and touch your belly
summary: A game of two-part directions using body parts.
how_to: Give two directions of the same kind: "Touch your nose and touch your belly." Do it with them at first, then let them try alone. Switch to "Give me the ball and give me your shoe" for variety.

title: Feelings in picture books
summary: Read books together and talk about the faces and feelings of the characters.
how_to: Pause on a page and describe what you see: "Look at his face. He looks sad; he dropped his ice cream." Connect it to your toddler's life: "Remember when you felt sad at the park?" A book about turning two, like 'Graham Turns Two' from the Lovevery Companion kit, works well.
materials: picture books with clear facial expressions

title: Play date: model concern
summary: Host a small play date and show your toddler how to notice and help when a friend is hurt.
how_to: Invite just one child and set out a simple shared activity, like a big paper taped to the floor with chunky crayons. If someone falls, say what you see: "Soraya fell down. I bet that hurt. Let's check on her." Take a snack break to reset and don't force interaction.
safety_notes: Check both children for food allergies before snacks.

title: Grow a feelings vocabulary
summary: Use specific emotion words like "disappointed," "proud," or "frustrated" to name your toddler's feelings.
how_to: When your toddler is upset or happy, name the feeling exactly: "You got the yellow car, not the blue one. You're disappointed." Try words such as frustrated, nervous, delighted, and proud as they come up during the day.

title: Animal match: same and different
summary: Your toddler matches animal figurines to picture tiles and sorts them by type.
how_to: Progresses from the month-19 figure match: more pairs, and sorting. Lay out a few picture tiles and the matching figurines. Match one together, then let your toddler finish. Later, sort animals into groups, such as farm and wild, and talk about what is the same and different.
materials: Montessori Animal Match (Lovevery Companion kit) or animal figurines with matching picture cards
safety_notes: Keep small figurines away from children who mouth toys.

title: Buckle barrel
summary: Your toddler opens and closes chunky buckles, using both hands together.
how_to: Show how to hold one side of a buckle still while pressing the other side in until it clicks. Then pinch to release. Let them repeat at their own pace; cheer the click rather than the speed.
materials: Buckle Barrel (Lovevery Companion kit) or a bag or high chair with no-pinch buckles
safety_notes: Use no-pinch buckles and keep straps short to avoid entanglement.

title: Toddler cleaning station
summary: Set up a low station with child-sized cleaning tools so your toddler can deal with spills on their own.
how_to: Put a spray bottle of mostly water, small cloths, a scrub brush, and a hand broom and dustpan in a caddy on a low shelf. When something spills, invite them to get the tools. Show where dirty cloths go when they're done.
safety_notes: Fill the spray bottle with water or a mild water-vinegar mix only; keep chemical cleaners locked away.

title: Clap the beat
summary: Clap along together to nursery rhymes so your toddler starts to feel the patterns in music.
how_to: Put your hands over your toddler's and clap to the beat of "Twinkle, Twinkle" or "Old MacDonald." Clap along whenever music plays. Try a simple A-B pattern too: clap, pat knees, clap, pat knees.

title: Flashlight shadow play
summary: Shine a flashlight on toy animals and natural objects and watch their shadows grow and shrink on the wall.
how_to: Dim the room and set a few plastic animals or pinecones on a table near a blank wall. Shine a flashlight on them and move it closer and farther away. Let your toddler hold the light and see what happens to the shadows.
safety_notes: Use a flashlight with a secured battery cover; keep small objects away from mouths.

title: Freeze dance
summary: Dance while the music plays and freeze when it stops, practicing quick starts and stops.
how_to: Explain: when the music plays we dance, when it stops we freeze. Show what freezing looks like, then play. Vary the length of the clips and the speed of the song, and strike a funny pose on each freeze. Wobbly freezes are fine.
safety_notes: Clear a space free of furniture corners.

title: Coach the climb with words
summary: Talk your toddler through climbing steps or a ladder instead of lifting them, so they learn how to place each hand and foot.
how_to: Watch quietly first. If they get stuck, remind them what worked before ("Last time you put your knee here"), describe what they're doing ("You're holding the rail"), and offer a "what if": "What if you put your foot on this step?" Afterward, describe what happened and offer another try.
safety_notes: Stay close enough to catch on anything higher than your toddler can safely fall.

title: Mosaic button board
summary: Your toddler presses chunky pegs into a board to make patterns, building finger strength and a precise pinch.
how_to: Show how to pinch a peg between thumb and pointer finger and push it into a hole. Let them make any design. Later, start a simple color row and see if they copy it.
materials: Mosaic Button Board (Lovevery Companion kit) or a large-peg pegboard
safety_notes: Pegs can be choking hazards; supervise.

title: Cap twist-off board
summary: Your toddler twists caps on and off a homemade board of pouch spouts or bottle tops.
how_to: Cut the spouts off 4–10 clean food pouches, push them through holes in a piece of cardboard, and glue or tape them on the back. Show how to unscrew and screw a cap. For a new challenge, tape the board under a table so they twist above their head.
materials: clean food-pouch tops with caps or bottle tops
safety_notes: Small caps are choking hazards; supervise and count caps at clean-up.

title: Play dough poke, squish, and roll
summary: Your toddler strengthens hands by poking, squishing, and rolling play dough with simple tools.
how_to: Give a ball of soft play dough with popsicle sticks, cookie cutters, and a spoon. Show how to poke, flatten, and roll a snake. If they're unsure about the texture, let them start by poking with a stick.
safety_notes: Play dough is not food; homemade dough is high in salt, so discourage eating it.

title: Who says moo? Sounds to pictures
summary: Make an animal sound and your toddler points to the matching picture, connecting hearing to seeing.
how_to: Progresses from the month-22 animal match: now the clue is a sound, not a figure. Lay out 3 or 4 animal pictures. Make one animal's sound and ask your toddler to point to the animal that makes it. Swap roles so they make a sound for you to find.

title: Put gestures into words
summary: Turn your toddler's gesture-plus-word into a two-word phrase they can copy.
how_to: When your toddler points at a speeding car and says "Fast!", reply "Fast car!" When they lift their arms and say "Mama," say "Mama up? Okay, Mama up!" as you pick them up. Say it warmly and don't make them repeat it.

title: Who is that? Photo walk
summary: Walk around your home naming the people in family photos with the question word "who."
how_to: Point to a photo and ask, stressing the word, "Who is that?" Then answer: "That's Grandma!" Do the same with characters in books. Once your toddler knows the routine, pause and let them point or name.

title: Say who's coming before you meet
summary: Before greeting friends or new people, tell your toddler who they are so the new situation feels safer.
how_to: When someone approaches, ask your toddler "Who is that?" and answer calmly: "That's our neighbor, Marta." Your toddler will watch your face and tone for cues, so greet warmly and let them hang back if they need to.

title: Name their pride
summary: When your toddler finishes something hard and looks at you, put words to the proud feeling.
how_to: Watch for the moment your toddler fits a tricky puzzle piece or climbs a step and grins at you. Describe the effort and the feeling: "You tried so hard and you did it. I bet you feel proud!" Focus on effort rather than a general "good job."

title: One-to-one muffin tin transfer
summary: Your toddler places one object into each cup of a muffin tin, an early math idea.
how_to: Progresses from month-22 tweezer transfer: now each item has exactly one spot. Put identical items, like small pumpkins or large pom poms, in a bowl beside a mini muffin tin. Let your toddler fill one per cup, and count softly as they go: "one, two, three."
materials: mini muffin tin or ice cube tray
identical items too large to swallow
safety_notes: Use items too big to be a choking hazard.

title: Chunky jigsaw puzzle
summary: Your toddler moves from shape puzzles to a simple, oversized jigsaw.
how_to: Start with only two or three pieces out and show how one edge fits into another. Let your toddler turn pieces to find the fit. When they finish it easily, try a large floor puzzle.
materials: Chunky Wooden Jigsaw Puzzle (Lovevery Companion kit) or a 2–4 piece chunky jigsaw

title: Dirty toys, clean toys
summary: Your toddler digs toys out of dirt and scrubs them clean in soapy water, learning about opposites.
how_to: Fill one bin with dirt and one with soapy water. Bury small toys in the dirt and let your toddler find them. Show how scrubbing in the water makes them clean and use the words "dirty" and "clean."
safety_notes: Supervise around water at all times; wash hands after soil play; use toys too large to swallow.

title: Sweep with a hand broom
summary: Your toddler sweeps crumbs into a pile and scoops them into a dustpan.
how_to: After a snack, hand your toddler a small broom and dustpan. Show the basics slowly: make a little pile, scoop it up, and tip it into the bin. Don't expect a perfect job; treat it as a regular part of cleaning up.

title: Water painting outside
summary: Your toddler paints the sidewalk, walls, and rocks with plain water and watches it dry.
how_to: Give your toddler a bucket of water and a chunky brush. Let them paint the ground, fences, and rocks, and fill the bucket themselves from a small pitcher. Point out how the sun dries their marks so they can paint again.
safety_notes: Supervise any bucket of water.

title: Finger marks in damp sand
summary: Your toddler draws lines and spirals in a tray of damp sand, smooths it, and starts again.
how_to: Spread damp sand in a shallow tray. Let your toddler draw with fingers or a stick, then show how to smooth the surface for a fresh start. Notice the marks out loud: "You made a long line and a circle."
safety_notes: Keep sand away from eyes and mouths; wash hands afterward.

title: Chalk jumping course
summary: Your toddler jumps between colored chalk circles when you call out a color.
how_to: Draw five colored chalk circles in a plus shape. Have your toddler stand in the middle and call, "Jump to red!" or "Jump to blue!" This makes them balance as they jump forward, backward, and sideways. Step instead of jump if both feet don't leave the ground yet.
safety_notes: Choose a flat surface away from traffic.

title: Kick the bag
summary: Balance a bean bag on your toddler's foot and have them kick it forward.
how_to: Set a bean bag on top of your toddler's foot and ask them to kick it as far as they can. This makes them balance on one leg. Mark how far it goes with chalk or a toy and try to beat it.
safety_notes: Offer a hand to hold if they wobble.

title: First snips with scissors
summary: Your toddler holds a strip of paper with one hand and snips it with child scissors.
how_to: Cut paper into narrow strips that take only one snip. Show how to open and close the scissors, then hold the strip so they can snip. Practice the opening-and-closing motion with tweezers if scissors are hard at first.
safety_notes: Use blunt-tip child scissors and supervise at all times; put them away after use.

title: Unscrew the jar
summary: Your toddler twists lids off small jars to find a surprise inside.
how_to: Progresses from the month-23 cap board to full-size lids that need a wrist turn. Put a small toy in two or three plastic jars with different lids. Show how to hold the jar with one hand and twist the lid with the other. Let them screw lids back on too.
materials: small toys or treats to hide
safety_notes: Use plastic jars, not glass, and hide objects too large to swallow.

title: Sock off, sock on
summary: Break dressing into small skills, starting with pulling off socks and pulling a shirt down.
how_to: Pick one mini-skill a day, such as pulling off a sock or tugging a shirt down over the belly. Name what they did: "You pulled your shirt down." Over time, add a step, like scrunching a sock and stretching it over the toes.

title: What is this? Naming in books
summary: Point to pictures in a book and ask open-ended questions so your toddler names what they see.
how_to: Progresses from month-20 story talk to asking your toddler to name things. Point to an object and ask, "What is this?" Wait several seconds. If they don't answer, name it and move on. Ask "Who was your favorite?" at the end, and let them stop whenever they want.

title: Judah's bear, your bear
summary: Pair your toddler's name with pronouns so they start to understand "I," "me," and "mine."
how_to: Use their name first, then connect it to the pronoun: "This is Judah's bear. This is your bear." Ask "Who is my helper? Judah is my helper!" to encourage them to use their own name. Pronouns usually come between 2 and 3.

title: Action words during play
summary: Play alongside your toddler using action phrases like "Let's roll the ball!" to deepen play and model verbs.
how_to: Sit with your toddler, follow what they look at or reach for, and use action words: "Roll the ball!" "Feed the bunny!" "Knock the tower down!" Over time, start the play together and then step back while they keep going.

title: Pass the ball circle
summary: Take turns passing a ball with your toddler, another child, and an adult.
how_to: Sit in a small circle and roll a ball to each other, saying the next person's name before each pass. Start with just you and your toddler, then add a friend and their grown-up. Cheer each turn.

title: Everything in its basket
summary: Give each toy type its own basket so your toddler can help put things back where they belong.
how_to: Set up a basket for blocks, another for stuffed animals, and a rack for books, each roomy enough not to overflow. At clean-up, sing a short tidy-up song and ask them to put one type away while you do the rest.

title: Shared floor mural
summary: Two children make marks side by side on one big sheet of paper and see their lines join up.
how_to: Tape a long sheet of paper to the floor or a wall and give each child their own chunky crayons. Let them scribble near each other. Talk about where their lines meet: "Your blue line touched Mia's red line."
safety_notes: Supervise crayon use for children who still mouth objects.

title: The ball is green
summary: Say the object first and the color second ("the ball is green") to help your toddler learn colors.
how_to: Instead of "look at the green ball," say "look, the ball is green." Use this order through the day with toys, clothes, and food. Don't worry if they call a red balloon "blue"; they are learning that color is a feature of things.

title: Block soup
summary: Symbolic play: your toddler fills a bowl with blocks and pretends to stir and eat "soup."
how_to: Put out a pot or bowl, a spoon, and a handful of small blocks. Start the game: "I'm making soup. Can you add some carrots?" Let them stir, serve, and feed a doll or you. Follow their ideas when they change the story.
safety_notes: Use blocks too large to swallow.

title: What's next? Setting the table
summary: Link two steps of a routine, like bringing the placemat and then the plate, using a pause and "What's next?"
how_to: Once your toddler can bring their placemat to the table, pause and wonder aloud, "What's next?" If they don't move, prompt, "Let's get your plate," and do it together. Repeat daily until they do both steps alone.

title: Watering the houseplants
summary: Your two-year-old waters houseplants with a small watering can and wipes up spills.
how_to: Show how to pour a little water at the base of the plant and watch it soak in. Explain, "Plants need water, but not too much." Keep a sponge and cloth nearby so your toddler can wipe up drips themselves.
safety_notes: Make sure the houseplants are non-toxic to children.

title: Squeeze your own orange juice
summary: Your toddler presses orange halves on a hand juicer and pours the juice into a cup.
how_to: Cut oranges in half and set them on a tray with a simple hand juicer, a small pitcher, and a cup. Show how to press and twist the orange, then pour. Keep a sponge on the tray for drips.
safety_notes: Adults do all cutting; citrus can sting small cuts.

title: Painting with nature
summary: Your toddler dips sticks, leaves, and pinecones in paint to see what marks each one makes.
how_to: Collect a few natural items on a walk. Pour a little washable paint into shallow dishes and tape down a big sheet of paper. Let your toddler press, drag, and dab with each item, and talk about the different textures and patterns.
safety_notes: Use non-toxic washable paint and avoid toxic plants.

title: Tiptoe animal rescue
summary: Your child stretches up on tiptoes to rescue soft toys taped high on a wall, then squats to put them away.
how_to: Tape a few soft toys to a wall just above your child's easy reach. Put a basket on the floor below. Ask them to rescue each animal on tiptoes, then squat down and drop it in the basket. Tiptoe work builds the leg muscles used for jumping.
safety_notes: Use painter's tape so paint doesn't peel; keep the area clear of furniture edges.

title: Animal walks from a bag
summary: Pull a toy animal from a bag and move like it: hop like a frog, waddle like a duck, stomp like an elephant.
how_to: Put a handful of toy animals in a bag. Take turns pulling one out, naming it, and moving like it. Show the movement first, then let your child copy. Include a frog or bunny so they practise two-footed hops.
safety_notes: Clear a soft open space; keep small figurines out of reach of children who still mouth objects.

title: Heavy-work helper
summary: Your child carries real loads, like a bag of groceries or a stack of books, to meet their need for big, effortful movement.
how_to: Hand your child a light grocery bag, a pile of board books, or a folded blanket to carry to where it belongs. Let them haul it all the way and set it down themselves. Thank them for the help.
safety_notes: Keep loads light enough to carry without straining; no glass or heavy cans.

title: Lock and key
summary: Your child fits a large key into a padlock and turns it to open and close the lock.
how_to: Offer one large, easy padlock with its key on a tray. Show slowly how to put the key in, turn, and pull the shackle open. Let your child repeat as often as they want.
safety_notes: Choose a chunky lock and key too big to swallow; supervise.

title: Pom-pom carton drop
summary: Your child pokes pom-poms through the spout of a milk carton and watches them come out a flap at the bottom.
how_to: Cut a flap at the bottom of a clean milk or juice carton. Show your child how to push a pom-pom through the top spout. Name each colour as it goes in, and later try sorting the pom-poms by colour.
safety_notes: Pom-poms are a choking hazard; supervise and put them away after play.

title: Zipper practice with a coin purse
summary: Your child opens and closes a small zippered purse, practising the same pinch-and-pull used on jackets.
how_to: Put a small treasure inside a zippered coin purse. Show how to hold the purse with one hand and pull the tab with the other. Let your child unzip, find the treasure, and zip it back. Give extra time when unzipping their own coat.
materials: small zippered purse or pencil case
one small toy (larger than a choke tube)
safety_notes: Use a treasure too big to swallow.

title: Action words with gestures
summary: Say common action words (eat, drink, wash, open, close) with a gesture so your child links the word to the action.
how_to: During the day, pair verbs with a clear gesture: lift a pretend cup for "drink", rub hands for "wash". Use the same word in different places, like washing hands, washing toys, washing laundry. When your child says one word, add the action: "Dog... dog runs!"

title: Silly body-part mix-ups
summary: Put a shoe on your hand or pyjama pants on your head and let your child tell you where they really go.
how_to: Pick a clothing item and put it on the wrong body part. Ask, "Does this go on my hand?" Wait for your child to point or say the right part. Then let them try a silly mix-up on you.

title: I hear with my little ear
summary: A listening version of I-spy: name a sound you hear and help your child find where it comes from.
how_to: Pause and say, "I hear with my little ear... the wind in the leaves." Point to the source: "Can you see the leaves moving?" Then ask what your child hears and name the sound with them. Play it at home, the park, or in a queue.

title: Take-turns block tower
summary: Build one tower together, one block each, until it falls.
how_to: Sit at a hard, level surface. Say, "First me, then you, then me, then you, until it falls." If your child adds two blocks, remind them gently: "Wait, it's my turn!" Don't straighten their blocks; they learn from the tumble.

title: How we walk inside
summary: A short grace-and-courtesy role-play that shows your child how to move safely indoors instead of correcting them after the fact.
how_to: At a calm moment, move silly, fast, then very slowly together and enjoy it. Then say, "Let me show you how we move in the house," and walk normally. Walk together, then ask your child to show you. Keep it short and end there.

title: Everyone in the mirror: make a face
summary: Make feeling faces together in a mirror and describe what each face looks like.
how_to: Stand at a mirror and say, "Everyone in the mirror look surprised!" Exaggerate the face, then describe it: "My eyebrows are up and my mouth is open." Try happy, angry, sleepy, sad. Let your child call out a feeling for you to make.
safety_notes: Use a shatterproof mirror or one fixed to the wall.

title: Two-step mirror directions
summary: Give simple two-part instructions at the mirror, like "First touch your ear, then touch your head."
how_to: Stand together at a mirror and do the moves with your child. Change one thing at a time: "First touch your nose, then your chin." Use the words first, then, next. If they're ready, try a harder one: "First touch your nose, then look up."
safety_notes: Use a shatterproof or wall-mounted mirror.

title: Nature soup
summary: Your child pours water over citrus slices and fresh herbs, stirs, and 'cooks' a fragrant pretend soup.
how_to: Put lemon and lime slices, orange peel, and mint or other herbs in a large bowl. Give your child a small jug of water and a whisk or slotted spoon. Let them pour and stir; the more they mix, the stronger the smell. Follow their lead if they serve you soup.
safety_notes: Supervise closely around water. Citrus can sting small cuts and eyes; wash hands after.

title: Fridge search
summary: Ask your child to find a named food in the fridge and hand it to you, ignoring everything else.
how_to: Open the fridge together and ask, "Do you see the carrots? Can you get them and give them to me?" Switch to another item: "Now find the cheese." Scanning for one thing and ignoring the rest is early flexible thinking.
materials: fridge items you need for a meal
safety_notes: Keep glass jars and heavy items on high shelves; hold the door.

title: Handwashing, step by step
summary: Teach the full handwashing routine: water on, wet, two pumps of soap, bubbles while singing, rinse, dry.
how_to: Set up a stool and a low towel hook. Go through each step with your child. Hold the dispenser while they pump and count "one, two." Sing a whole song while scrubbing, then rinse well and dry. A picture card by the sink helps them remember.
materials: hand towel on a low hook
safety_notes: Test water temperature yourself; you control the hot tap. Keep the stool stable on a non-slip mat.

title: Bubble-wrap painting with a mirror
summary: Your child runs fingers and brushes through paint on taped-down bubble wrap, watching their hands in a mirror.
how_to: Tape a large sheet of bubble wrap to an outdoor table. Squirt small circles of washable paint on it and prop a mirror nearby. Let your child explore with fingers, and press paper on top for prints if they want. Leave it out for repeat visits, then hose it off.
safety_notes: Use washable, non-toxic paint. Shatterproof mirror only. Supervise if your child still mouths things.

title: First flower arranging
summary: Your child pours water into a small vase through a funnel and places flower stems in it, then chooses where to display it.
how_to: Set a tray with a small vase, funnel, small jug of water, sponge, and a few flowers you have already trimmed. Show slowly: pour water through the funnel, wipe drips with the sponge, place one stem at a time. Let your child pick the spot for the vase.
safety_notes: Adult trims stems at this age. Choose non-toxic flowers and an unbreakable or sturdy vase; wipe spills to prevent slips.

title: Lily-pad crossing
summary: Your child crosses a pretend lake by stepping from paper 'lily pads' without touching the water, then tries jumping between them.
how_to: Tape sheets of paper or tissues to a carpeted floor a short step apart. Tell your child the floor is a lake and the pads keep their feet dry. Once stepping is easy, invite them to jump from pad to pad with both feet. Move pads closer if jumps fall short.
safety_notes: Tape pads down firmly on carpet so they don't slide; avoid smooth hard floors.

title: DIY bottle bowling
summary: Roll a ball at water-weighted bottles and take turns setting them back up.
how_to: Fill 3-6 plastic bottles with a little water or sand and screw the lids on tight. Set them in a triangle and sit a few steps away. Take turns rolling the ball. Between rounds, your child stands the bottles back up, on dot stickers if you want to mark the spots.
safety_notes: Tighten lids well so water or sand can't spill or be swallowed.

title: Taking off socks and pants: the last step
summary: Let your child do the final step of undressing themselves, like pulling socks off their toes or pant legs off their feet.
how_to: Around 26 months many children can start taking clothes off. Do the tricky part (buttons, getting pants past the knees) and leave the last step to them. Use elastic waists and loose socks. Give extra time when you're not rushed.
safety_notes: Have your child sit on the floor or a low stool so they don't topple.

title: Your turn to turn the page
summary: Read your child's favourite book for the hundredth time and let them turn each page.
how_to: Keep favourite books on a low shelf your child can reach. When they bring one, settle in and let them turn the pages one at a time. Pause on a picture and ask them to name what you point to. Repeat reading builds enjoyment and confidence.

title: Threading large rings
summary: Your child slides big rings onto a cord with a wooden threader, a first step toward bead stringing.
how_to: Offer a few large wooden rings and a cord with a stiff wooden threader on the end. Show how to push the threader through a ring and pull it along. Let them fill the cord, then slide the rings off and start again.
safety_notes: Supervise cords at all times and put them away after play (strangulation risk).

title: Fill-in-the-blank songs
summary: Leave out the action word in a song your child knows and let them fill it in.
how_to: Sing a familiar song and stop before the action word: "If you're happy and you know it, ______." Wait a few seconds. If they're stuck, do the action (clap) as a hint. Try other songs with clear verbs: row, jump, wash, splash.

title: Where, oh where?
summary: A finding game that models pronouns: "Where is Nana? There she is! Where is her shoe? There it is!"
how_to: Sing-song, "Where, oh where, oh where is Charlie?" then, "There you are!" Find family members, then their things: "Where is her shoe?" When your child says "Mine!", model more: "Yes, that is your cup. This cup is mine."

title: Sound walk
summary: Walk around your neighbourhood listening for sounds and naming them together.
how_to: On a slow walk, stop and ask, "What do you hear?" Name sounds out loud: "I hear a bird chirping. I hear a car engine." Let your child point to the source. Honk, knock, bark, beep are great early sound words.
safety_notes: Hold hands near roads and driveways.

title: Spot someone who needs help
summary: Point out when someone needs help, like a pet's empty water bowl, and invite your child to be the helper.
how_to: Name the need out loud: "Kitty's water bowl is empty. Let's fill it for her." Or, "Your sister can't reach her jacket. Should we help?" When your child helps, say what it did: "Thank you for picking up my glasses. Now I can see." Expect messy help and thank them anyway.
materials: everyday household needs (pet bowl, dropped items)

title: Gentle hands and the waiting hand
summary: Short grace-and-courtesy lessons: how to touch friends gently and how to wait to talk by placing a hand on an adult's arm.
how_to: Show gentle hands by softly stroking your child's arm: "This is how we touch our friends." For the waiting hand, place your hand on another adult's arm, have them cover it with theirs, then turn and say, "Thank you for waiting." Role-play both several times.

title: Find the two that match: black and white
summary: Your child picks out two black objects from a set of three that differ only in colour.
how_to: Between 26 and 29 months many children start matching black with black and white with white. Lay out three identical items, two black and one white (crayons, straws, socks). Say, "Let's find the two that are the same." Ask why they chose them, even if they can't explain yet.
safety_notes: Avoid small items your child could swallow.

title: Knobbed puzzles and shape posting
summary: Simple knobbed puzzles and a shape sorter let your child work out which piece fits which space.
how_to: Put out one small knobbed puzzle (a few circles or shapes) and one shape sorter. Show once, slowly. Let your child try, and wait before helping; turning a piece until it fits is the work. Rotate puzzles often and keep only a few choices out.
safety_notes: Check shape-sorting beads and puzzle knobs are too large to swallow; supervise.

title: Pretend to be Mum or Dad
summary: Your child acts out an adult's routine, like grabbing keys and a bag to leave, or taking a pretend work call.
how_to: Leave out a few safe real-life props: an old bag, a coat, a toy phone, a shopping basket. When your child pretends to be you, play along and ask what they're doing. Role play makes them think about what a character says and does, and they repeat words they've heard.
safety_notes: Remove straps, cords, and real keys or coins from props.

title: Reggio nature table
summary: Set out a low, open collection of natural treasures your child can touch, sort, and use in play.
how_to: Gather pinecones, bark, shells, stones, and leaves from walks. Arrange them in an open tray or shallow drawer at your child's height. Let them use the pieces however they like: as 'food', in block scenes, pressed into clay. Add new finds after each outing.
safety_notes: Choose pieces too big to swallow; check for sharp edges and wash finds before use.

title: Spice paints
summary: Your child paints with homemade paints made from ground spices like turmeric, paprika, and cinnamon.
how_to: Put a tablespoon of each spice in a small cup and stir in just enough water to make a paste. Give your child a brush and thick paper. Talk about each colour and smell as they paint.
materials: turmeric, paprika, cinnamon or other ground spices
safety_notes: Spices stain and can sting eyes; cover clothes and wash hands after. Skip hot spices like chilli.

title: Wipe a spill, sweep a pile
summary: Your child wipes up small spills with a cloth and sweeps crumbs into a pile with a small broom and dustpan.
how_to: Keep a small cloth and a child-size broom and dustpan where your child can reach them. When a spill happens, hand them the cloth and show slow wiping. For sweeping, show the basics: make a little pile, scoop it up, put it in the bin.
safety_notes: Clean up broken glass yourself; dry wet floors to prevent slips.

title: Three-part obstacle course
summary: Your child crawls through a tunnel, runs across the room, then climbs over a big cushion, switching how they move at each stage.
how_to: Set up three stations in a row: a tunnel (or a sheet over two chairs), an open stretch to run, and a large floor cushion to climb. Walk through it together once, naming each step: "Crawl, then run, then climb." Let your child repeat it, and change the order when it gets easy.
materials: play tunnel or sheet over chairs
safety_notes: Keep the run path clear of furniture corners; put cushions on a non-slip surface.

title: Sweep the buttons into the square
summary: Your child uses a broom to sweep scattered large buttons or pom-poms into a taped square on the floor.
how_to: Tape a big square on the floor. Scatter large buttons or pom-poms around it. Show how to hold the broom with two hands and push the pieces into the square. Sweeping toward a target practises motor planning, working out how to move the body to finish a job.
safety_notes: Use pieces too large to swallow and supervise; collect them all after play.

title: Russian nesting doll
summary: Your child twists and pulls apart a wooden nesting doll to find the smaller dolls inside, then nests them back in order.
how_to: Offer a nesting doll with 3-5 pieces. Show slowly how to grip top and bottom and twist or pull apart. Line the dolls up by size, then rebuild from the smallest. Let your child work out the order; it takes practice.
safety_notes: Check that the smallest doll is too big to be a choking hazard.

title: Felt balls with tongs
summary: Your child moves felt balls from a bowl with fingers or tongs, strengthening the grip used later for pencils.
how_to: Put a bowl of felt balls and a second empty bowl (or a peg tree) on a tray. Younger toddlers use fingers; show older ones how to squeeze small tongs to pick up and release each ball. Let them return the balls and repeat.
materials: 2 small bowls or a peg tree
safety_notes: Felt balls are a choking hazard for children who mouth objects; supervise.

title: Coat off and onto a low hook
summary: When you come home, your child takes off their own coat and hangs it on a hook at their height.
how_to: Fit a low hook by the door and a small bench or stool for sitting. Unzip or unbutton the tricky part, then let your child pull their arms out and hang the coat by its loop. Keep only two pairs of shoes to choose from on a mat or rack.
safety_notes: Fit hooks with rounded ends below your child's eye level, or use a peg rail.

title: Add one word
summary: When your child says a two-word phrase, repeat it back with one more word added.
how_to: Listen for phrases like "Dog run." Echo with a small addition: "Dog runs fast!" or "Yes, the dog is running." Don't ask them to repeat it; just model the longer version. This builds on last month's action-word play.

title: Washing-up song
summary: Change the words of a familiar tune to describe what your child is doing, like washing plates.
how_to: While your child washes dishes or toys, sing to "The Farmer in the Dell": "It's time to wash the plates, the plates are dirty and need a bath..." Use vivid words as they work: sticky, wet, shiny, slippery. Swap in whatever they're doing: wiping, sweeping, stirring.
safety_notes: Use unbreakable dishes and lukewarm water; stay close and wipe up splashes so the floor isn't slippery.

title: Vocabulary basket: name it, find it
summary: Use a basket of related objects (dogs, fruit, tools) to teach new names with a Montessori three-period lesson.
how_to: First, name each object simply: "Labrador," and let your child hold it. Then play finding games: "Can you find the dalmatian?" or match objects to picture cards. Skip asking "What is this?" at this age so you don't set them up to get it wrong; just re-present names they miss.
safety_notes: Choose figures too large to swallow.

title: The turn ball
summary: Pass a soft ball back and forth; only the person holding it gets to talk, jump, or dance.
how_to: Call a soft ball the "turn ball." Explain that whoever holds it gets a turn and the other person waits. Keep turns very short (under 10 seconds) so your child gets it back quickly. Prompt them to hand it back. Try it for talking, silly faces, or jumping.

title: Playdate set up for side-by-side play
summary: Prepare a small playdate with toys in multiples so two-year-olds can play near each other without fighting over one item.
how_to: In the morning, tell your child who's coming and when; let them help prepare a snack. Put away special new toys. Set out several of the same thing (cars, cups, shakers). If a conflict starts, say, "It will be your turn when your friend is finished. What could we do while you wait?" Expect mostly parallel play.
safety_notes: Check snacks and toys suit both children's ages and any allergies.

title: Name the proud feeling
summary: When your child does something on their own, pause, let them feel it, then name it: "You look so proud."
how_to: Watch for small wins, like putting on shoes. Wait a moment before speaking so the pride is theirs. Then say, "You did that all on your own! You look proud." If they struggle, focus on effort: "That strap is tricky. Let's do it together."

title: Colour drop: white or red?
summary: Your child drops objects into one of two clear containers depending on colour, moving from black-white to white-red.
how_to: Put a white object in one clear container and a red one in another. Give your child a small mixed pile and ask, "Which container do you think this goes in?" This builds on last month's black-and-white matching. Comparing two primary colours (red vs yellow) usually comes later.
materials: 6-10 white and red objects (blocks, pegs, straws)
safety_notes: Use objects too big to swallow.

title: Puzzles with less picture help
summary: Try layer or construction puzzles where the board doesn't show the exact piece picture, so your child has to work out shapes.
how_to: Swap a matching-picture puzzle for one with less visual support, like a layer puzzle. Offer the bottom layer's pieces first. Wait before helping; turning and testing pieces is the problem-solving. Return to an easier puzzle if frustration builds.
materials: layer puzzle or puzzle without picture under pieces

title: First the red bell, then the yellow
summary: Give two-step music instructions using coloured bells or xylophone bars.
how_to: Use coloured pat bells or a coloured xylophone. Say, "First tap the red one, then the yellow one," and wait. Do it together the first few times. When two steps are easy, add a third.

title: Child-size dishwashing station
summary: After eating, your child scrapes, washes, rinses, and racks their own unbreakable dishes.
how_to: Set two shallow basins on a low table or stool: soapy water and rinse water, plus a small drying rack and towel. Show the order once: scrape scraps into the bin, pump a little soap on a cut-down sponge, wash, rinse, rack. Fill basins before meals and empty them after.
safety_notes: Use only unbreakable dishes and lukewarm water; supervise around water and wipe floor spills.

title: Lavender playdough on a tile
summary: Your child presses and rolls dried lavender sprigs and flowers into plain playdough on a smooth tile.
how_to: Make or buy plain playdough. Set a smooth tile as the work space with a small dish of dried lavender and loose dried petals. Let your child press, roll, and mix freely. The tile defines the space and gives a smooth surface.
safety_notes: Dried flowers are not food; supervise children who mouth materials. Check for wheat allergy with homemade dough.

title: Musical water jars
summary: Tap jars holding different amounts of water and listen to how the pitch changes.
how_to: Fill 3-5 same-size jars with different water levels. Show how to tap the side gently with a metal spoon. Add or pour off water together to 'tune' them. Ask which sound is high and which is low.
safety_notes: Glass can break; supervise closely, tap gently, and work on a towel on a low table.

title: Red light, green light
summary: Run on "green light", stop fast on "red light", holding up a red or green object as a visual cue.
how_to: Use a hallway or open space. Hold up something green and call "Green light!" for running, then something red and "Red light!" for stopping. Show what stopping looks like. If stopping is hard, teach your child to jump to a stop with both feet. Swap roles so they're the caller.
materials: red and green objects (paper, bean bags, balls)
safety_notes: Play in a clear, enclosed space away from roads.

title: Foot painting
summary: Your child stomps, slides, and hops across paper dotted with paint, using their whole body to make marks.
how_to: Tape or weigh down a long strip of paper outdoors. Add small dollops of washable paint a few inches apart. Let your child try with a finger first, then feet. Suggest pressing firmly, sliding, and hopping from spot to spot.
safety_notes: Painted paper is slippery; hold hands for hops and keep the area flat. Use washable, non-toxic paint.

title: Carry a full cup across the room
summary: Your child fills a cup at one side of the room and walks slowly to pour it into a bowl on the other side.
how_to: Put a small tub of water (or a play sink) on one side and a large bowl on the other. Give a two-step instruction: "Fill your cup, then pour it in the bowl." Walking with a full cup builds balance and body control. Keep a towel handy.
materials: tub of water or play sink
safety_notes: Supervise around water and dry spills right away to prevent slips.

title: Buttons into tiny lidded pots
summary: Your child sorts small coloured buttons into matching small pots and opens and closes each lid.
how_to: Offer 3-4 small coloured containers with lids and a dish of buttons in the same colours. Show how to take off a lid, drop in a button that matches, and put the lid back on. The small size makes lids a fine-motor challenge.
materials: 3-4 small lidded containers in different colours
safety_notes: Small buttons are a choking hazard; use only with close supervision and store out of reach.

title: First scissor snips
summary: Your child practises making single snips with toddler-safe scissors on small strips of paper.
how_to: Draw a smiley face on your child's thumbnail; if they can see it, their thumb is up. Give small paper strips, or tape one end to the table so they can focus on cutting. Expect single snips, not lines. Try modelling dough or junk mail too.
safety_notes: Use blunt-tip child scissors; sit at a table and supervise the whole time. Store scissors out of reach.

title: Lift-the-flap nature book
summary: Your child lifts flaps and turns pages in a book about caring for bugs, pets, and plants.
how_to: Read a sturdy lift-the-flap book like 'When You Love a Living Thing'. Let your child lift each flap and turn each page themselves. Point and ask them to name what they find underneath.

title: Wh- questions in pretend play
summary: Ask who, what, and where during pretend play to help your child put ideas into words.
how_to: Join your child's play and ask open questions: "There's a fire! What do we need? We need... water!" Pause long enough for them to answer. Accept one or two words and repeat back a fuller sentence.
materials: pretend props your child already uses

title: My words book
summary: Record the words your child says and turn them into a homemade picture book to read together.
how_to: For a week, jot down every word your child says. Print or draw a picture for each and staple the pages into a simple book. Read it together and let them name the pictures. Model correct pronunciation without correcting: "Here's your spaghetti!"
safety_notes: Adult handles the stapler.

title: My turn, your turn colour game
summary: Take turns pulling coloured pieces from a bag, modelling "my turn", "your turn", "I got blue, you got green."
how_to: Put coloured pieces (dots, blocks, pom-poms) in a bag. Take one out, place it, and say, "I got a blue one. Your turn!" Let your child pull one. Narrate with pronouns: "You got green! This one is mine."
safety_notes: Use pieces too big to swallow.

title: Tea party for two
summary: Set out a small tea set at a playdate so two children can pour and pretend side by side.
how_to: Put a toy tea set with a small jug of water on a low table. If your child offers you a cup, redirect: "I wonder if Henry wants some tea." Step back and let them pour for each other. Expect short bursts of shared play.
safety_notes: Supervise water play and wipe spills; use only clean drinking water if they sip.

title: Emotion match: see it, make it, name it
summary: Your child looks at a feeling face on a card, copies it in a mirror, and says the feeling.
how_to: Show a picture of a face (from emotion cards or a book). Make the face together in a mirror and name it: "Surprised!" Seeing, copying, and naming engages both sides of the brain. This takes last month's mirror faces a step further by matching a picture.
materials: emotion cards or photos of faces
safety_notes: Use a shatterproof mirror.

title: Hello and goodbye role-play
summary: A grace-and-courtesy lesson where you act out greeting a visitor and saying goodbye before it happens for real.
how_to: At a calm time, use a toy or another adult as the 'visitor'. Show how to open the door, wave or say hello, and invite them in. Then act out goodbye. Let your child play both host and visitor. Keep it short and fun.
materials: soft toy or family member as visitor

title: Sort by colour, then switch the rule
summary: Your child sorts red and green items by colour, then sorts the same items by type, practising flexible thinking.
how_to: Mix red and green buttons with red and green blocks. Set out two bowls and ask your child to sort by colour. Then tip them together and ask them to sort buttons in one bowl, blocks in the other. If something lands in the wrong bowl, say lightly, "Oops, the buttons go here."
materials: red and green buttons or dots
safety_notes: Small buttons are a choking hazard; supervise.

title: What will happen? Balance-scale predictions
summary: Use a toy balance scale to ask your child to predict which side will go down or whether an object will fit in the pail.
how_to: Hold a heavy and a light ball over the pails and ask, "What will happen if I drop them?" Watch which side drops. Try "Will this fit?" with toys of different sizes, and end with a silly one: "Will Daddy fit?"
materials: objects of different weights and sizes
safety_notes: Use objects too big to swallow.

title: Picture matching cards
summary: Your child matches pairs of picture cards (balls, farm animals, tools) and talks about each picture.
how_to: Start with a small set, 4-6 pairs, from one theme. Lay one of each in a row and hand your child the matches to place. Name each picture as they work. Rotate themes when interest drops.

title: Laundry helper: find the sock pairs
summary: Your child pairs socks from the clean laundry, looking at colour and size.
how_to: Pull four contrasting socks from the laundry, maybe two big and two small in different colours. Ask, "Can you find the socks that go together?" Let them also open the machine door, pull clothes out, and put their dirty clothes in the basket at bedtime.
safety_notes: Keep detergent pods and liquid out of reach; supervise around machine doors.

title: DIY light table
summary: Make a simple light table from a frosted storage bin and lights, then explore how household objects look lit from below.
how_to: Put tap lights or a string of white fairy lights inside a frosted plastic bin and close the lid. Gather slightly see-through things: plastic letters, coloured lids, glass gems, beads on a string. Let your child look at each item before and after it goes on the light. Talk about colours and shapes.
materials: frosted plastic storage bin with lid
tap lights or white string lights
safety_notes: Gems and beads are a choking hazard; supervise. Keep cords tidy and use low-heat LED lights.

title: Peel a clementine
summary: Your child peels a clementine, puts the peel in one bowl and the segments in another, then eats them.
how_to: Set a tray with a clementine and two bowls. Start the peel for them with a small opening. Show slowly: peel a piece, put it in the peel bowl, separate segments into the other bowl. Compost the peel together.
safety_notes: Remove seeds and watch for choking; have your child sit while eating.

title: Frog hops, crab walks, flamingo stands
summary: A harder round of animal moves: squat-and-hop like a frog between 'lily pads', crab-walk sideways, and balance like a flamingo.
how_to: Draw chalk circles or set stepping stones as lily pads. Show a frog hop: squat all the way down, then jump with both feet. Add crab walking on all fours sideways and a one-second flamingo stand holding your hand. This builds on the animal walks from a few months ago with harder movements.
safety_notes: Use a soft, flat surface; hold hands for one-foot balancing.

title: Beach ball into the hoop
summary: Take turns lifting a beach ball overhead and throwing it into a hula hoop or chalk circle.
how_to: Lay a hula hoop or draw a chalk circle a few steps away. Show how to lift the ball over your head with both hands and throw. Take turns and cheer each throw. Overhead throwing works the arms, shoulders, back, and core that steady the body for later writing.
safety_notes: Use a light, soft ball and a clear space.

title: Squeeze-a-lemon lemonade
summary: Your child twists a fork inside half a lemon to squeeze the juice through a sieve, then adds water and honey.
how_to: Set a tray with half a lemon, a fork, a small sieve over a cup, a small jug of water, and a little honey. Show how to push the fork into the lemon and twist it back and forth over the sieve. Your child pours in water, adds a spoon of honey, stirs, and drinks.
safety_notes: Honey is fine after age 1. Lemon juice stings cuts and eyes. Adult cuts the lemon.

title: Scoop and sort by colour
summary: Your child uses a slotted spoon to scoop floating coloured objects out of shallow water and drop each into a matching cup.
how_to: Add a few inches of water to a shallow tub with floating items in 3-4 colours (foam shapes, plastic blocks, flowers). Set out cups in matching colours. Show how to scoop one item and put it in its cup. This is a step up from last month's dry colour sorting.
safety_notes: Never leave a child alone with water, even shallow. Use items too big to swallow.

title: Pants down, pants up
summary: Your child practises pulling elastic-waist pants down and back up on their own.
how_to: Between 28 and 32 months many children can pull pants up to the waist. Help get feet through the leg holes facing the right way, then let your child pull up. Practise pulling down too, a skill they'll use for toileting. Builds on taking socks off from earlier months.
safety_notes: Have your child sit or hold a wall for balance.

title: Start a story, let them finish
summary: Begin a simple story and pause for your child to say what happens next.
how_to: Say, "Once upon a time, there was a unicorn who loved to explore. Where did the unicorn go?" Wait. Accept any answer and keep going with it: "To the park! What did she see there?" Stop while it's still fun.

title: Story stones
summary: Smooth stones painted with simple pictures (a dog, a house, the sun) become prompts for naming and telling stories.
how_to: Paint or draw simple pictures on a handful of smooth stones and let them dry. Put them in a basket. Your child picks a stone and names the picture; you string a few together into a tiny story: "The dog ran to the house." Let them choose the order.
safety_notes: Use stones larger than your child's mouth; seal paint and let it dry fully.

title: I notice, I wonder
summary: Use rich words and "I notice... I wonder..." statements, plus action rhymes like "Open, Shut Them," to grow your child's vocabulary.
how_to: Swap general words for specific ones: "Oh, a tulip!" instead of "a flower." Think out loud: "I notice the snail is slow. I wonder where it's going." Sing short repetitive rhymes such as "Open, Shut Them" so your child tunes into word sounds.

title: Practise drop-off and pick-up
summary: Role-play the goodbye ritual for childcare or preschool, letting your child play both the child and the parent.
how_to: Choose a short goodbye ritual: a hug, a kiss, one more for luck. Act it out with soft toys, then with your child as the parent leaving. Tell them all feelings are okay and they can squeeze their soft toy or ask the teacher for help. Start talking about a new school no more than a week ahead.

title: Space for two in the block corner
summary: Give each child their own small building board so siblings or friends can build side by side without knocking each other's work down.
how_to: Set a small board or tray for each child in the block area. Each builds on their own board. Give words to use: "I'm still playing with this. When I'm finished you can have a turn." and "May I have a turn please?" Step in only if needed.

title: How does the character feel?
summary: While reading, stop to talk about how a character feels and what might help.
how_to: When something happens in a story, pause: "Oh no, Max fell down. How do you think he feels? How can you tell?" Then ask, "What might make him feel better?" Talking about characters' feelings builds understanding of emotions and empathy.

title: Unload the dishwasher by category
summary: Ask your child to hand you dishes by changing categories: "one of your dishes", "a plate", "something silver".
how_to: Open the dishwasher together. Ask for items using different rules each time: owner, shape, colour. Add two steps: "Find a spoon, then put it in the drawer." Switching between categories practises flexible thinking.
materials: dishwasher or drying rack with unbreakable dishes and spoons
safety_notes: Remove knives and glassware first.

title: Sunny-day shadow play
summary: Your child moves toys, sticks, and their own body to see how shadows change shape and size.
how_to: On a sunny day, find a plain wall or path. Let your child hold up toys, sticks, or their hands and watch the shadows. Ask them to make a shadow bigger or smaller by moving closer or farther. Make up a little story with the shadow shapes.
safety_notes: Use sun protection; remind your child not to look at the sun.

title: Peg board: sort by height and colour
summary: Your child places pegs on a geometric peg board, first freely, then sorting by height and colour.
how_to: Offer a peg board with pegs of different colours and heights. Let your child place them freely at first. Later show one row of same-colour pegs and see if they continue it, then try ordering by height.
safety_notes: Check that pegs are too large to swallow.

title: Kitchen jobs: tear, stir, crinkle-cut
summary: Your child does real kitchen jobs: tearing lettuce, stirring batter, and cutting banana with a crinkle cutter.
how_to: Get out all ingredients and tools first. Offer a step stool or learning tower at the counter. Give one job at a time: tear lettuce into a bowl, stir with a towel wrapped under the bowl so it doesn't slide, cut banana with a crinkle cutter. Thank them at the meal: "These are the bananas you cut."
materials: learning tower or stable step stool
safety_notes: Keep sharp knives and hot surfaces out of reach; secure the stool; watch for food allergies.

title: Clay with natural materials
summary: Your child pushes clay onto pinecones and bark or presses sticks and seed pods into it to make simple sculptures.
how_to: Give a fist-sized lump of air-dry or natural clay on a board, with a few pinecones, bark pieces, and sticks. Clay moves differently from playdough, so let your child spend days just squashing and making 'sausages'. Over time they'll pinch off pieces and join them with sticks.
safety_notes: Clay is not food; wash hands after. Check natural materials for sharp edges.

title: Stop-and-go shakers
summary: Shake shakers fast on "Go!" and freeze on "Stop!", then switch between loud and quiet.
how_to: Give your child a shaker and keep one yourself. Say "Go!" and shake fast together, then "Stop!" and freeze. Next, drum loud on a box, then tap quietly, and invite them to copy. Music games like this help build impulse control.
safety_notes: Seal homemade shakers well so small fillings can't spill out.

title: Red light, green light: new colours
summary: Add new 'lights' to the game: blue means hop, yellow means walk slowly, purple means walk backward, pink means walk sideways.
how_to: Start with the red and green version your child already knows. Add one new colour at a time with a matching object: blue light for hopping on two feet, yellow for slow walking, purple for walking backward. Let your child be the caller. On walks, connect it to real traffic lights.
materials: red, green, blue, yellow, purple objects or paper
safety_notes: Play in a safe open space like a yard or park, away from traffic.

title: Shovel, load, and haul
summary: Your child shovels sand, soil, or snow into buckets, carries them, and pulls a loaded wagon or sled, the 'maximum effort' work toddlers crave.
how_to: Give a child-size shovel and buckets in a sandpit, garden, or snow. Let them fill, carry, and dump as many times as they like. Add a wagon or sled to pull, loaded with toys for extra challenge. This builds on earlier heavy-work carrying with bigger outdoor loads.
safety_notes: Keep loads manageable; dress for the weather; supervise near roads and slopes.

title: First sewing card
summary: With a blunt, pre-threaded darning needle, your child stitches along a diagonal row of holes in thick card.
how_to: Punch 5-6 holes in a diagonal line on thick card. Thread a blunt darning needle with double thread and knot it. Show slowly: push the needle halfway, turn the card, say "Look!", pull it through away from you. Repeat each hole. Store the needle in a needle case.
safety_notes: Use only a blunt needle; teach your child to point it away from their body; supervise and store the needle and thread out of reach.

title: Draw on the wall (on paper)
summary: Your child draws with small crayon pieces on large paper taped to a wall, which builds shoulder strength and a better grip.
how_to: Tape butcher paper to a wall at your child's shoulder height. Offer broken crayon pieces or rock crayons instead of long crayons; small, round tools train the thumb-and-finger grip. Draw a circle yourself and let them try if they want.
safety_notes: Use non-toxic crayons; supervise small crayon pieces with children who mouth objects.

title: Mash-it guacamole
summary: Your child scoops avocado into a bowl, squeezes lime with a fork, and mashes it all with a fork.
how_to: Cut an avocado in half and a lime in half. Show how to slide a fork between skin and flesh to release the avocado into a bowl, then let your child do the second half. Squeeze lime with the fork, then mash and mix. Serve with crackers.
safety_notes: Adult cuts and removes the avocado stone. Lime stings cuts and eyes. Check for allergies.

title: I spy a beginning sound
summary: A relaxed Montessori sound game: "I spy something that begins with /m/... a marigold!"
how_to: Start with one familiar object and say its first sound, not the letter name: "I'm going to eat something that begins with /s/ /s/ /s/: a strawberry!" Play for a couple of minutes during meals, gardening, or laundry. Model sounds yourself without quizzing: "I'm folding this /sh/ /sh/ shirt." Stop if interest fades and try again later.

title: Act out the book
summary: While reading a book about actions, pause so your child can do and name what the people in the pictures are doing.
how_to: Choose a book with clear actions (clapping, jumping, waving). At each page, ask, "What is she doing?" and then do it together: "She's jumping! Let's jump!" Name the action in a short sentence each time.

title: Ask about yesterday
summary: Ask specific questions about recent events to invite short sentences and a back-and-forth chat.
how_to: Instead of "What did you do today?", ask "What book did you read with Grandma?" or "What did the dog do at the park?" Listen, then reply and ask one more question to keep the exchange going. Model correct words without correcting.

title: Scarf and shaker dance party
summary: At a playdate, put out shakers and play scarves with music so children can dance and play near and with each other.
how_to: Lay out enough scarves and shakers for every child. Put on catchy family music. Dance along, then step back. Notice when children copy each other or start a shared game, and name it: "You're both spinning!"
safety_notes: Clear the space of tripping hazards; scarves are for supervised play only.

title: Set the table: one napkin each
summary: Your child sets out napkins for the family, counting one for each person.
how_to: Before a meal, hand your child the exact number of napkins and say, "One for each plate." Count together as they place them. Next time, ask them to count family members first to work out how many they need. Keep napkins where they can reach them.

title: Sort by colour only
summary: Your child puts all yellow shapes in one bowl and all green shapes in another, ignoring whether they're circles, squares, or triangles.
how_to: Give two containers and a mix of shapes in two colours. Ask your child to sort by colour only. If a piece goes in the wrong bowl, take it out, name the colour, point to the right bowl, and let them try again. Add a third colour when it gets easy. This extends last month's colour sorting.

title: Mystery bag: guess by touch
summary: Your child reaches into a bag without looking, feels an object, and guesses what it is.
how_to: The sense of identifying things by touch starts developing around 2.5. Put 3-4 familiar objects in a cloth bag (a spoon, a ball, a toy car). Your child reaches in, feels one, and names it before pulling it out. Start with very different shapes, then try pairs to match by feel.
safety_notes: Use objects too big to swallow, with no sharp edges.

title: Shadow theatre guessing game
summary: Hold familiar objects behind a lit screen and let your child guess what they are from the shadow.
how_to: Line a shoebox lid or cardboard frame with tracing paper and shine a flashlight from behind. Hold up one familiar object at a time behind the screen and ask, "What could it be?" Move it closer to and farther from the light to make the shadow grow and shrink. Then let your child be the shadow-maker.
safety_notes: Remind your child never to shine the flashlight in anyone's eyes.

title: Folding cloths
summary: Your child folds napkins and washcloths along marked lines, a classic Montessori job that suits children around 2.5.
how_to: Show how to fold a cloth napkin in half with one fold, slowly, and let your child copy. To help, draw fold lines on washcloths with a fabric pen: one straight line first, later a diagonal. Then let them put the folded cloths away in a low drawer.

title: Mark-making with unexpected tools
summary: Your child makes marks with sticks, feathers, straws, and brushes on surprising surfaces like foil, sandpaper, or cardboard.
how_to: Gather a mix of tools (sticks, feathers, sponges, brushes) and surfaces (paper, foil, cardboard, sandpaper). Add paint, chalk, or crayons. Let your child explore how each tool marks each surface. Listen to how they describe it and note what they return to.
safety_notes: Use washable, non-toxic media; check sticks and feathers for sharp ends.

title: Grow a seed
summary: Your child plants seeds, waters them, and watches them sprout, keeping track of changes over weeks.
how_to: Put sunflower or bean seeds on damp cotton wool in a clear cup, or plant them in a small pot of soil. Let your child water and check them each day. Ask questions together: How long will they take? Do they need light? Take a photo or draw the changes in a small notebook, then pot seedlings into soil.
safety_notes: Seeds are a choking hazard; adult hands them out one at a time. Wash hands after handling soil.

title: Hop and toss with hoops and bean bags
summary: Jump into hoops and toss bean bags to build two-foot jumping and aim.
how_to: Lay two or three hoops (or tape circles) on the floor in a row. Show your child how to jump with both feet from one hoop into the next. Then stand at the edge and take turns tossing a bean bag into a hoop.
safety_notes: Use on a non-slip surface; hoops on hard floors can slide when stepped on.

title: Color tag
summary: Run, hop, or tiptoe to the color you call out.
how_to: Tape three colored sheets of paper on walls around a room. Name a color and have your child run and tag it. Switch to hopping or tiptoeing, then try a two-step direction like 'first red, then yellow.' Let your child call the colors for you.
safety_notes: Clear furniture corners and loose rugs from the running path.

title: Walk the line, then jump the rope
summary: Start a mini obstacle course by walking a line and jumping over a rope.
how_to: Make a straight line on the floor or sidewalk with tape or chalk. Ask your child to walk along it heel-to-toe. At the end, lay a rope flat and have them jump over it with both feet. Add one new element at a time once they succeed.
safety_notes: Keep the rope flat on the ground; never tie it up as a hurdle at this age.

title: Twist & Pivot Pattern Puzzle, one tower at a time
summary: Twist colored pieces on and off a puzzle post to build wrist and finger strength.
how_to: Start with the puzzle assembled and let your child twist pieces off. Put away all but the easiest tower and show how to turn pieces clockwise to put them on. Add one piece from each tower once that feels easy.
safety_notes: Expect frustration; stop before it turns into a meltdown.

title: Cereal pattern necklace
